27: MCP Server
28: Official MrScraper MCP server for retrieving web pages, web search, and account usage. Connect AI clients or run the open-source server locally.
29: MrScraper MCP is the official Model Context Protocol server for MrScraper.
30: It connects AI clients to web page retrieval, web search, and your account
31: usage.
32: MrScraper MCP server source code on GitHub
33: · Install the @mrscraper/mcp npm package
34: The server exposes seven tools:
35: status
36: Return the raw account status API response without summarizing, redacting body fields, or adding calculated fields.
37: scrapeHtml
38: Retrieve the raw HTML of a page. Browser rendering is optional.
39: scrapeMarkdown
40: Retrieve a page as Markdown. Including HTML also enables browser rendering and returns both outputs as JSON.
41: getScreenshot
42: Capture a base64 screenshot of the full page or top viewport. Browser rendering is always enabled.
43: scrapeBrand
44: Extract a website's colors, typography, logos, and social links as JSON.
45: scrapeJson
46: Extract structured JSON from a page using a natural-language prompt. Append Json Schema: and a JSON schema to shape the output.
47: webSearch
48: Search the web and return ranked results with titles, URLs, descriptions, and sources.
49: Use the hosted Streamable HTTP endpoint for a managed connection, or run the
50: published MCP package locally through Streamable HTTP or stdio.
51: Package information
52: This page documents @mrscraper/mcp version 0.5.0. Its seven tools share their descriptions, inputs, and defaults with the MrScraper CLI, SDKs, and integrations. 0.5.0 replaced scraperAPI with scrapeHtml, scrapeMarkdown, and getScreenshot, added scrapeBrand and scrapeJson, renamed the inputs to camel case, and changed the OAuth scopes. See Migration from the previous tool set.
53: Capabilities
54: Page Retrieval
55: Retrieve a known URL as HTML, Markdown, or a screenshot, with optional
56: browser rendering, real-device routing, proxy controls, selector waiting,
57: and retry limits.
58: Brand and JSON Extraction
59: Extract a website's colors, typography, logos, and social links, or
60: structured JSON from a natural-language prompt.
61: Web Search
62: Search the web for ranked results, for a chosen country and up to 100
63: results at a time.
64: Account Status
65: Read the subscription, token limit, token usage, remaining tokens, and rate
66: limit.
67: Managed Endpoint
68: Connect to the hosted MCP endpoint through Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1
69: browser sign-in.
70: Structured Tool Results
71: Receive a consistent response envelope in MCP structured content.
72: Interactive Widgets
73: Render search results and an account usage meter in hosts that support MCP
74: Apps.
75: Requirements
76: A MrScraper account
77: An MCP client with Streamable HTTP support
78: An API key only when the client cannot use
79: OAuth 2.1 or when running the server locally
80: Quick start with the hosted server
81: Add the hosted endpoint
82: Configure a Streamable HTTP server named mrscraper with no credential:
83: {
84: "mcpServers": {
85: "mrscraper": {
86: "type": "http",
87: "url": "https://mcp.mrscraper.com/mcp"
88: }
89: }
90: }
91: Use this exact URL, including the /mcp path.
92: Sign in
93: Connect or reload the MCP server. Your client follows the OAuth 2.1
94: challenge, opens MrScraper in your browser, and asks you to approve

Detect the current MCP client and use its native Streamable HTTP setup to add a server named mrscraper at exactly https://mcp.mrscraper.com/mcp with no static credential. 195: Authentication
196: ConnectionCredential source
197: Hosted Streamable HTTPOAuth 2.1 browser sign-in, or an API key fallback
198: Self-hosted Streamable HTTPOAuth 2.1 access token, or Authorization: Bearer <MrScraper API key>
199: Local stdioMRSCRAPER_API_KEY, then MRSCRAPER_API_TOKEN
200: The hosted server publishes OAuth 2.1 protected-resource metadata and challenges
201: unauthenticated clients to start browser sign-in. Access tokens are issued for
202: the exact https://mcp.mrscraper.com/mcp resource. A tool called without its
203: required scope returns 403 insufficient_scope, and your client can offer to
204: grant the missing permission.
205: ScopeTools
206: scrape:readscrapeHtml, scrapeMarkdown, getScreenshot, scrapeBrand, scrapeJson, and webSearch
207: account:readstatus
208: These are the only application scopes the server advertises; the
209: authorization server also offers offline_access for refresh tokens. Clients
210: take the scopes from the server's metadata, so don't pin scopes in client
211: configurations.
212: OAuth connections that already hold scrape:read keep working without
213: reconnecting; scrape:write is no longer needed by any tool. Connections
214: without scrape:read must reconnect and approve it to run the scraping and
215: search tools; status still uses account:read.
216: API keys remain supported for clients without OAuth and carry full account
217: authority, so no scope is enforced against them. Authentication stays at the
218: transport layer; tools never accept credentials as arguments.

276: Security behavior
277: HTTP authentication is enabled by default.
278: Credential-bearing response headers are filtered from tool output.
279: Credential metadata in scraping and search responses is redacted, and
280: network errors redact signed query credentials.
281: status preserves every field of the account status response body,
282: including account identity and billing identifiers. Only credential-bearing
283: response headers are removed.
284: Browser-origin requests are accepted from trusted local origins, from
285: claude.ai and chatgpt.com, and from exact
286: values configured through MRSCRAPER_ALLOWED_ORIGINS.
287: Tool calls receive the caller's authenticated OAuth token or API key through
288: the MCP transport rather than through tool arguments.

323: Common response envelope
324: Every tool returns the same envelope in MCP structuredContent and as
325: formatted JSON in a text content block:
326: {
327: "content": [
328: {
329: "type": "text",
330: "text": "[Formatted JSON matching structuredContent]"
331: }
332: ],
333: "structuredContent": {
334: "status_code": 200,
335: "data": "<html><body>Example page content...</body></html>",
336: "headers": {
337: "content-type": "text/html; charset=utf-8"
338: }
339: }
340: }
341: FieldTypeDescription
342: status_codenumber or nullHTTP status returned by the MrScraper service, or null when the request ends before an HTTP response arrives.
343: dataJSON value, string, or nullThe API response body, as parsed JSON or text. Its field names are not converted.
344: headersobjectResponse headers with credential-bearing headers filtered out.
345: errorstring, when presentRequest failure summary.
346: status preserves the complete account status body without adding summary
347: fields.
348: Error handling
349: HTTP and network failures set isError: true on the MCP tool result and
350: include error in the envelope. Network failures use status_code: null.
351: Invalid inputs, including inputs a tool does not define, are rejected before
352: any upstream call. Authentication and missing OAuth scopes are enforced by the
353: HTTP transport before a tool runs.
354: Tool reference
355: Tool names, descriptions, inputs, and defaults match the MrScraper CLI, SDKs,
356: and integrations. Inputs use camel case and are sent to the API under the same
357: names. Tools authenticate through the MCP connection and do not accept a token
358: argument.
359: ToolTitleOAuth scopereadOnlyHintopenWorldHint
360: statusAccount Statusaccount:readtruefalse
361: scrapeHtmlScrape HTMLscrape:readfalsetrue
362: scrapeMarkdownScrape Markdownscrape:readfalsetrue
363: getScreenshotGet Screenshotscrape:readfalsetrue
364: scrapeBrandScrape Brandscrape:readtruetrue
365: scrapeJsonScrape JSONscrape:readfalsetrue
366: webSearchWeb Searchscrape:readtruetrue
367: Every tool sets destructiveHint: false. scrapeHtml, scrapeMarkdown,
368: getScreenshot, and scrapeJson are not marked read-only because
369: saveResult can save their results to your dashboard. The six scraping and
370: search tools use tokens from your plan.
371: Examples use https://example.com as the sample target. Replace it for your
372: use case. Response examples show the envelope from structuredContent, with
373: selected keys and types observed in live API responses. Values are
374: placeholders; page content, base64 images, and arrays are abbreviated. Actual
375: responses may contain additional fields.
376: Shared parameters
377: HTML, Markdown, screenshots, and JSON extraction share url, timeout,
378: geoCode, proxyCountry, super, waitUntil, proxy, maxRetries, and
379: saveResult. Page defaults are 300 seconds, US geolocation and proxy country,
380: real-device routing off, and dashboard saving off. Omitted retry limits mean no
381: limit.
382: HTML, Markdown, and screenshots additionally accept blockResources,
383: waitForSelector, and returnCookie. JSON extraction does not accept these
384: controls. Browser rendering is optional for HTML, Markdown, and JSON;
385: screenshots always enable it. Markdown with HTML also enables browser
386: rendering.
387: The six scraping and search tools send GET requests to the Scraper API with
388: their inputs as query parameters:
389: GET https://api.mrscraper.com
390: Each tool's table lists its complete inputs.

435: scrapeHtml
436: Retrieve the raw HTML of a page. Browser rendering is optional.
437: The request sets html=true, markdown=false, and screenshot=false.
438: Parameters
439: ParameterTypeDefaultDescription
440: urlstringRequiredAbsolute HTTP or HTTPS URL of the page to process.
441: timeoutinteger300Page load timeout in seconds, from 1 to 300. The HTTP request allows 30 additional seconds.
442: geoCodestring"us"Two-letter country code to load the page from, sent in lowercase.
443: proxyCountrystring"us"Two-letter country code of the proxy server, sent in lowercase.
444: superbooleanfalseWhether to route the request through real devices.
445: waitUntilstring: domcontentloaded, load, networkidle0, networkidle2"domcontentloaded"Navigation completion event to wait for: domcontentloaded, load, networkidle0, or networkidle2.
446: proxystringOmittedCustom proxy URL used to load the page.
447: maxRetriesintegerOmittedMaximum number of retries, as a nonnegative integer. Omit this parameter for no limit.
448: saveResultbooleanfalseWhether to save the result to the dashboard Result tab.
449: blockResourcesbooleanfalseWhether to block images, fonts, and stylesheets while loading the page.
450: waitForSelectorstringOmittedWait for the page to contain the specified CSS selector before returning the result.
451: returnCookiebooleanfalseWhether to include browser session cookies in the response.
452: browserRenderingbooleanfalseWhether to render the page in a browser before returning the result.
453: warmStartbooleanfalseWhether to enable warm start for more reliable scraping, at the cost of additional latency.

456: "name": "scrapeHtml",
457: "arguments": {
458: "url": "https://example.com",

472: "content-type": "text/html; charset=utf-8"

641: "prompt": "Extract the first 2 items with title and price. Json Schema: {\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"title\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"price\":{\"type\":\"string\"}},\"required\":[\"title\",\"price\"]}}",
642: "browserRendering": true
643: }
644: }
645: Response
646: Extraction results are in the API body's data field and follow the requested schema. Response metadata includes thread_id, token_usage, status, error, runtime, and cookies. html, markdown, and screenshot can be empty strings when not requested.
647: {
648: "status_code": 200,
649: "data": {
650: "success": true,
651: "data": [
652: {
653: "title": "Example item",
654: "price": "10.00"
655: }

658: "token_usage": 1,

661: "screenshot": "",

663: "error": "",
664: "runtime": 1.23,
665: "cookies": []
666: },
667: "headers": {
668: "content-type": "application/json"
669: }
670: }
671: webSearch
672: Search the web and return ranked results with titles, URLs, descriptions, and sources.
673: Parameters
674: ParameterTypeDefaultDescription
675: querystringRequiredSearch query text, trimmed before sending, containing 1 to 1000 characters.
676: countrystring"us"Two-letter country code to search from, sent in lowercase.
677: numResultsinteger10Number of search results to request, as an integer from 10 to 100. Fewer results may be returned.
678: The HTTP deadline is fixed at 120 seconds. It is not a service parameter.
679: The request uses action=websearch.
680: Example
681: {
682: "name": "webSearch",
683: "arguments": {
684: "query": "site:example.com documentation",
685: "country": "id",
686: "numResults": 20
687: }
688: }

690: The API body contains success, message, a data array, and tokenUsage. Each result includes rank, title, url, description, and source.

693: "data": {
694: "success": true,

699: "title": "Example result",
700: "url": "https://example.com",
701: "description": "Example result description.",
702: "source": "example.com"

27: CLI
28: Install, authenticate, and use the MrScraper CLI to retrieve pages as HTML, Markdown, or screenshots, extract brand details and structured JSON, search the web, and check account status.
29: The MrScraper CLI provides terminal access to the seven MrScraper services, with browser sign-in and optional agent skill setup. Its commands share their descriptions, parameter meanings, and defaults with the MCP server, the SDKs, and the other integrations. This guide covers installation, authentication, output, environment variables, programmatic usage, and complete command details.
30: CommandDescription
31: statusReturn the raw account status API response without summarizing, redacting body fields, or adding calculated fields.
32: scrape-htmlRetrieve the raw HTML of a page. Browser rendering is optional.
33: scrape-markdownRetrieve a page as Markdown. Including HTML also enables browser rendering and returns both outputs as JSON.
34: get-screenshotCapture a base64 screenshot of the full page or top viewport. Browser rendering is always enabled.
35: scrape-brandExtract a website's colors, typography, logos, and social links as JSON.
36: scrape-jsonExtract structured JSON from a page using a natural-language prompt. Append Json Schema: and a JSON schema to shape the output.
37: web-searchSearch the web and return ranked results with titles, URLs, descriptions, and sources.
38: init, login, auth status, logout, and setup skills are configuration commands.
39: Requirements
40: Node.js 20 or newer
41: A MrScraper account for browser login, or an API key for non-interactive use
42: Package information
43: This page documents version 0.7.1. Version 0.7.0 replaced scraperAPI with scrape-html, scrape-markdown, and get-screenshot, replaced account with status, added scrape-brand and scrape-json, renamed webSearch to web-search, and switched to a three-skill pack. See Migrating from 0.6.x. See @mrscraper/cli on npm for the current published version.
44: Installation
45: Install only the CLI globally:
46: npm install -g @mrscraper/cli@latest
47: mrscraper --version
48: Install the CLI and the MrScraper agent skill pack for every detected harness:
49: npx -y @mrscraper/cli@latest init --all
50: Install for one harness:
51: npx -y @mrscraper/cli@latest init --agent codex
52: Supported IDs are claude-code, cursor, codex, grok, hermes, opencode, openclaw, pi, and omp.
53: The skill pack contains three skills: mrscraper for setup and account usage, mrscraper-fetch for page retrieval, and mrscraper-serp for web search.
54: Copyable AI setup prompt
55: Read and follow https://github.com/mrscraper-com/cli/blob/main/skills/mrscraper/SKILL.md
56: For an agent-controlled, non-interactive setup, skip authentication during bootstrap and start login separately:
57: npx -y @mrscraper/cli@latest init --agent codex --yes --skip-auth
58: mrscraper auth status --json
59: mrscraper login
60: CLI and skills only
61: mrscraper init installs the CLI and skill pack. It does not install or configure MCP. See MCP Server for hosted MCP setup.
62: init parameters
63: ParameterDefaultScopeBehavior
64: --api-key <key>—LocalSaves the supplied key during bootstrap instead of browser login.
65: --allenabledLocalInstalls skills for every supported harness detected on this machine.
66: --agent <id>—LocalInstalls skills for one supported harness, even when its detection directory is absent.
67: -y, --yesoffLocalKeeps bootstrap non-interactive. Missing authentication is left for a later login.
68: --skip-installoffLocalDoes not install the current CLI version globally.
69: --skip-authoffLocalPerforms no authentication step.
70: --skip-skillsoffLocalDoes not install the skill pack.
71: --dry-runoffLocalPrints intended actions without installing, authenticating, or copying skills.
72: Refresh only the skills with mrscraper setup skills. It accepts --agent <id> for one harness and --dry-run; without --agent, it targets detected harnesses.
73: mrscraper setup skills
74: mrscraper setup skills --agent hermes
75: mrscraper init --all --yes --skip-auth --dry-run
76: Native plugins (optional)
77: Native agent plugins are maintained separately from the CLI for ChatGPT and Codex and Claude. See Claude Code setup for installing the Claude plugin.
78: Choose one skill installation method
79: If npx ... init already installed the MrScraper skills for an agent, skip plugin installation for that agent. Enabling both methods can load duplicate copies of the same skills.
80: Verifying installation
81: After completing installation, verify that the CLI binary and commands are accessible in your environment:
82: mrscraper --version
83: mrscraper auth status --json
84: mrscraper status
85: A successful status call confirms that the CLI can load its authentication and reach the MrScraper service.
86: Skill pack reloading
87: Restart an agent harness or open a new terminal session after installing skills so it reloads the skill pack properly.
88: Authentication
89: Browser login
90: mrscraper login
91: The CLI opens the MrScraper login page, waits for browser approval, and saves a dedicated API key in ~/.mrscraper/auth.json. Keep mrscraper login running until approval completes. Set MRSCRAPER_HOME to change the containing directory.
92: API-key login
93: mrscraper login --api-key "$MRSCRAPER_API_KEY"
94: For automation, set an environment variable instead of saving a key:
95: export MRSCRAPER_API_KEY="YOUR_TOKEN"
96: Authentication precedence for service commands is:
97: Command --token
98: MRSCRAPER_API_KEY
99: MRSCRAPER_API_TOKEN
100: ~/.mrscraper/auth.json
101: --token is sent in request headers, never in the request URL.
102: login parameters
103: ParameterDefaultScopeBehavior
104: --api-key <key>—LocalSaves this API key and does not open browser login.
105: --token <key>—LocalDeprecated alias for login's --api-key.
106: --no-browseroffLocalPrompts a human for an API key; requires an interactive terminal.
107: --no-openoffLocalPrints the browser sign-in URL without launching it. The CLI still waits for approval.
108: --timeout <seconds>180LocalMaximum time to wait for browser approval.
109: Auth status and logout
110: mrscraper auth status reports the credential currently available to the CLI. It reads the local configuration without sending a test request. JSON output uses the credential_configured field, plus source for an environment variable or path for a saved key:
111: {
112: "credential_configured": true,
113: "auth_type": "api_key",
114: "path": "/home/user/.mrscraper/auth.json"
115: }
116: mrscraper logout deletes local credential files. It does not revoke an API key remotely.
117: Output
118: Every service command prints a JSON envelope to stdout:
119: {
120: "status_code": 200,
121: "data": "<html><body>Example page content...</body></html>",
122: "headers": {
123: "content-type": "text/html; charset=utf-8"
124: }
125: }
126: status_code contains the HTTP response code.
127: data contains the API response body. JSON bodies are parsed; other bodies, such as HTML or Markdown text, remain strings. Field names are returned as the API sends them.
128: headers contains response headers. Credential-bearing headers are filtered, and known credential metadata in scraping and search JSON is redacted. status preserves its body fields.
129: Failed API calls print a JSON envelope with error and exit non-zero. HTTP failures keep the status in status_code; network failures use null.
130: Progress messages use stderr so stdout stays machine-readable. Invalid arguments fail before any request.
131: Save large output with shell redirection:
132: mrscraper scrape-html https://example.com > result.json
133: mrscraper scrape-markdown https://example.com | jq -r '.data'
134: Response examples on this page show selected keys with placeholder values. Actual responses may contain additional fields.
135: Environment variables
136: VariableDefaultPurpose
137: MRSCRAPER_API_KEY—Preferred API-key environment override.
138: MRSCRAPER_API_TOKEN—Alternative API-key environment override.
139: MRSCRAPER_HOME~/.mrscraperCredential directory override.
140: MRSCRAPER_API_BASE_URLhttps://api.app.mrscraper.com/api/v1Development override for status and login.
141: MRSCRAPER_FETCH_BASE_URLhttps://api.mrscraper.comDevelopment override for scraping and search commands.
142: The CLI also loads a .env file from the current working directory.
143: Shared parameters
144: Service options use kebab-case. Run mrscraper <command> --help to see the options a command accepts. Every service command also accepts --token <key>.
145: Page controls
146: scrape-html, scrape-markdown, get-screenshot, and scrape-json accept these options. Page defaults are 300 seconds, US geolocation and proxy country, real-device routing off, and dashboard saving off. Omitted retry limits mean no limit.
147: ParameterAPI fieldTypeDefaultDescription
148: <url>urlstringRequiredAbsolute HTTP or HTTPS URL of the page to process.
149: --timeouttimeoutinteger300Page load timeout in seconds, from 1 to 300. The HTTP request allows 30 additional seconds.
150: --geo-codegeoCodestring"us"Two-letter country code to load the page from, sent in lowercase.
151: --proxy-countryproxyCountrystring"us"Two-letter country code of the proxy server, sent in lowercase.
152: --supersuperbooleanfalseWhether to route the request through real devices.
153: --wait-untilwaitUntilstring: domcontentloaded, load, networkidle0, networkidle2"domcontentloaded"Navigation completion event to wait for: domcontentloaded, load, networkidle0, or networkidle2.
154: --proxyproxystringOmittedCustom proxy URL used to load the page.
155: --max-retriesmaxRetriesintegerOmittedMaximum number of retries, as a nonnegative integer. Omit this parameter for no limit.
156: --save-resultsaveResultbooleanfalseWhether to save the result to the dashboard Result tab.
157: Loading controls
158: scrape-html, scrape-markdown, and get-screenshot also accept these options. scrape-json does not.
159: ParameterAPI fieldTypeDefaultDescription
160: --block-resourcesblockResourcesbooleanfalseWhether to block images, fonts, and stylesheets while loading the page.
161: --wait-for-selectorwaitForSelectorstringOmittedWait for the page to contain the specified CSS selector before returning the result.
162: --return-cookiereturnCookiebooleanfalseWhether to include browser session cookies in the response.
163: Browser rendering is optional for HTML, Markdown, and JSON; screenshots always enable it. Markdown with HTML also enables browser rendering.
164: CLI command list
165: status
166: Return the raw account status API response without summarizing, redacting body fields, or adding calculated fields. It takes no service parameters, and its HTTP deadline is fixed at 600 seconds. --json is accepted for compatibility; JSON is already the default.
167: mrscraper status
168: mrscraper status | jq '.data.data.tokenUsage'
169: The API body contains message and data. Account details remain nested in data, including subscriptionItem and scraperAllowance, so the envelope exposes them at data.data.
170: {
171: "status_code": 200,
172: "data": {
173: "message": "Example response",
174: "data": {
175: "id": "ACCOUNT_ID",
176: "tokenLimit": 100000,
177: "tokenUsage": 2500,
178: "stripeStatus": "active",
179: "user": {
180: "name": "Example user",
181: "email": "user@example.com",
182: "isVerified": true
183: },
184: "subscriptionItem": {
185: "name": "Example plan",
186: "tokenLimit": 100000
187: },
188: "scraperAllowance": {
189: "remaining": 97500,
190: "plans": [{ "remaining": 97500 }]
191: }
192: }
193: },
194: "headers": {
195: "content-type": "application/json; charset=utf-8"
196: }
197: }
198: scrape-html
199: Retrieve the raw HTML of a page. Browser rendering is optional.
200: Accepts page controls, loading controls, and:
201: ParameterAPI fieldTypeDefaultDescription
202: --browser-renderingbrowserRenderingbooleanfalseWhether to render the page in a browser before returning the result.
203: --warm-startwarmStartbooleanfalseWhether to enable warm start for more reliable scraping, at the cost of additional latency.
204: mrscraper scrape-html https://example.com --browser-rendering --warm-start \
205: --wait-for-selector 'body' --timeout 120 --max-retries 0
206: The default response body is HTML text. Additional controls can cause the API to return JSON; the returned structure is preserved.
207: Scrape HTML usage is based on runtime and bandwidth. Resource blocking can reduce bandwidth for text-focused pages, and --max-retries limits retry usage. See the Token Plan for the complete calculation.
208: scrape-markdown
209: Retrieve a page as Markdown. Including HTML also enables browser rendering and returns both outputs as JSON.
210: Accepts page controls, loading controls, and:
211: ParameterAPI fieldTypeDefaultDescription
212: --browser-renderingbrowserRenderingbooleanfalseWhether to render the page in a browser before returning the result.
213: --warm-startwarmStartbooleanfalseWhether to enable warm start for more reliable scraping, at the cost of additional latency.
214: --htmlhtmlbooleanfalseWhether to include the page HTML in the response.
215: mrscraper scrape-markdown https://example.com --html --warm-start
216: The default response body is Markdown text. With --html, data is an object containing both outputs:
217: {
218: "status_code": 200,
219: "data": {
220: "html": "<html>...</html>",
221: "markdown": "# Example page\n\n..."
222: },
223: "headers": {
224: "content-type": "application/json"
225: }
226: }
227: get-screenshot
228: Capture a base64 screenshot of the full page or top viewport. Browser rendering is always enabled.
229: Accepts page controls, loading controls, and:
230: ParameterAPI fieldTypeDefaultDescription
231: --screenshotscreenshotstring: full, top"full"Screenshot area to capture: full for the entire page or top for the top viewport.
232: --no-htmlhtmlbooleantrueSets html=false. Whether to include the page HTML in the response.
233: --markdownmarkdownbooleanfalseWhether to include the page Markdown in the response.
234: mrscraper get-screenshot https://example.com --screenshot top --no-html --markdown
235: mrscraper get-screenshot https://example.com --no-html | jq -r '.data.screenshot' | base64 -d > page.png
236: The response body contains a base64 screenshot and the requested page outputs. The API can still include HTML when HTML output is disabled.
237: {
238: "status_code": 200,
239: "data": {
240: "html": "<html>...</html>",
241: "screenshot": "BASE64_PNG_DATA",
242: "markdown": "# Example page\n\n..."
243: },
244: "headers": {
245: "content-type": "application/json; charset=utf-8"
246: }
247: }
248: scrape-brand
249: Extract a website's colors, typography, logos, and social links as JSON. It takes only the URL; page controls are not accepted. The HTTP deadline is fixed at 120 seconds.
250: mrscraper scrape-brand https://example.com
251: The API body contains message and a data object with job_id, status, url, final_url, brand, and error. Brand details are at data.data.brand.
252: {
253: "status_code": 200,
254: "data": {
255: "data": {
256: "job_id": "JOB_ID",
257: "status": "succeeded",
258: "url": "https://example.com",
259: "final_url": "https://example.com",
260: "brand": {
261: "name": "Example brand",
262: "colors": { "background": "#ffffff", "text": "#222222" },
263: "typography": { "body": { "font_family": "Example font" } }
264: },
265: "error": null,
266: "bundle_url": null
267: },
268: "message": "Example response"
269: },
270: "headers": {
271: "content-type": "application/json"
272: }
273: }
274: scrape-json
275: Extract structured JSON from a page using a natural-language prompt. Append Json Schema: and a JSON schema to shape the output.
276: Accepts page controls and:
277: ParameterAPI fieldTypeDefaultDescription
278: --promptpromptstring"Extract all data as complete as possible."Instructions describing the data to extract. Append Json Schema: and a JSON schema to shape the output.
279: --browser-renderingbrowserRenderingbooleanfalseWhether to render the page in a browser before returning the result.
280: --htmlhtmlbooleanfalseWhether to include the page HTML in the response.
281: --screenshotscreenshotbooleanfalseWhether to include a base64 screenshot in the response.
282: mrscraper scrape-json https://example.com --browser-rendering \
283: --prompt 'Extract the first 2 items with title and price. Json Schema: {"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","properties":{"title":{"type":"string"},"price":{"type":"string"}},"required":["title","price"]}}'
284: Extraction results are in the API body's data field and follow the requested schema. Response metadata includes thread_id, token_usage, status, error, runtime, and cookies. html, markdown, and screenshot can be empty strings when not requested.
285: {
286: "status_code": 200,
287: "data": {
288: "success": true,
289: "data": [{ "title": "Example item", "price": "10.00" }],
290: "thread_id": "THREAD_ID",
291: "token_usage": 1,
292: "html": "",
293: "markdown": "",
294: "screenshot": "",
295: "status": "Results ready",
296: "error": "",
297: "runtime": 1.23,
298: "cookies": []
299: },
300: "headers": {
301: "content-type": "application/json"
302: }
303: }
304: web-search
305: Search the web and return ranked results with titles, URLs, descriptions, and sources. The HTTP deadline is fixed at 120 seconds.
306: ParameterAPI fieldTypeDefaultDescription
307: <query>querystringRequiredSearch query text, trimmed before sending, containing 1 to 1000 characters.
308: --countrycountrystring"us"Two-letter country code to search from, sent in lowercase.
309: --num-resultsnumResultsinteger10Number of search results to request, as an integer from 10 to 100. Fewer results may be returned.
310: mrscraper web-search "site:example.com documentation" --country id --num-results 20
311: The API body contains success, message, a data array, and tokenUsage. Each result includes rank, title, url, description, and source.
312: {
313: "status_code": 200,
314: "data": {
315: "success": true,
316: "message": "Example response",
317: "data": [
318: {
319: "rank": 1,
320: "title": "Example result",
321: "url": "https://example.com",
322: "description": "Example result description.",
323: "source": "example.com"
324: }
325: ],
326: "tokenUsage": 1
327: },
328: "headers": {
329: "content-type": "application/json; charset=utf-8"
330: }
331: }
332: Programmatic use
333: The package exports the low-level functions used by the commands: scrapeHtml, scrapeMarkdown, getScreenshot, scrapeBrand, scrapeJson, webSearch, and getSubscriptionAccountApi.
334: import { scrapeMarkdown, webSearch, getSubscriptionAccountApi } from "@mrscraper/cli";
335: const token = process.env.MRSCRAPER_API_KEY;
336: const page = await scrapeMarkdown({ token, url: "https://example.com" });
337: console.log(page.data);
338: const results = await webSearch({ token, query: "books", country: "us", numResults: 10 });
339: for (const item of results.data.data) console.log(item.rank, item.title, item.url);
340: const status = await getSubscriptionAccountApi(token);
341: console.log(status.data.data.tokenUsage);
342: The functions take a single options object and return the same envelope the commands print. Options use camelCase, and the JavaScript option for super is superMode. getSubscriptionAccountApi takes the token as its only argument. Programmatic calls require an explicit token and do not load saved CLI credentials or .env files. For an application client, prefer the Node.js SDK.
343: Troubleshooting
344: For missing credentials, run mrscraper login or set MRSCRAPER_API_KEY.
345: For slow pages, increase --timeout up to 300 seconds. scrape-brand and web-search have fixed 120-second deadlines.
346: Use --help on a command to inspect its accepted options.
347: Migrating from earlier versions
348: From 0.6.x
349: Version 0.7.0 replaces the three 0.6.x data commands with seven service commands. The old command names are not kept as aliases.
350: 0.6.x0.7.x
351: mrscraper scraperAPI <url>mrscraper scrape-html <url>
352: mrscraper scraperAPI <url> --no-html --markdownmrscraper scrape-markdown <url>
353: mrscraper scraperAPI <url> --markdownmrscraper scrape-markdown <url> --html
354: mrscraper scraperAPI <url> --no-html --screenshotmrscraper get-screenshot <url> --no-html
355: mrscraper scraperAPI <url> --home-pagemrscraper scrape-html <url> --warm-start
356: mrscraper webSearch <query>mrscraper web-search <query>
357: mrscraper accountmrscraper status
358: scraperAPI({ token, url, ... })scrapeHtml, scrapeMarkdown, or getScreenshot
359: account({ token })getSubscriptionAccountApi(token)
360: status prints the raw API body as JSON. The 0.6.x summary at data.account, the terminal dashboard, and the --pretty and --no-color options are gone.
361: status and web-search no longer accept --timeout.
362: Defaults changed: page --timeout is now 300, --geo-code and --proxy-country default to us, and an omitted --max-retries means no limit.
363: --no-use-proxy, --bypass-proxy, --cookie-jar, --headers, --token-cap, --stream, --discard-token-secret, --no-browser-rendering, and --save are removed. Use shell redirection instead of --save.
364: The skill pack changed from four skills (mrscraper, mrscraper-scraper-api, mrscraper-account, mrscraper-web-search) to three (mrscraper, mrscraper-fetch, mrscraper-serp). Run mrscraper setup skills to refresh installed skills.
365: Earlier versions
366: 0.5.x to 0.6.0: the format-specific 0.5.x commands (scraperHtml, scraperMarkdown, getScreenshot, scraperJson, scraperMultiplePage, scraperSitemap, scrapeBrand, getBrand) were merged into scraperAPI. Upgrade directly to the 0.7.x commands above.
367: From 0.4.x: webSearch moved to action: "websearch" with --country and --num-results, and the MRSCRAPER_SYNC_BASE_URL setting was removed.

87: Frequently Asked Questions
88: Everything you need to know about plans, billing, and getting started with MrScraper.
89: What do I get on the Free plan?
90: Free costs nothing - no credit card required. It's the fastest way to try scraping, proxies and AI extraction before upgrading.
91: Can I change plans later?
92: Yes. Upgrade from Free to Essential anytime from your account's billing settings, or move to Enterprise by booking a call.
93: How do I get my API Token?
94: Sign in to the dashboard, open your account settings, and copy the token from the API Token page. Every API request authenticates with it, and the getting-started guide in the docs walks through your first call.
95: Can I use MrScraper without coding?
96: Yes. The visual scraper and AI Mode let you point at a page, describe the data you want, and get structured results without writing code. The API and SDKs are there when you want to automate further.
97: Why is my scrape not returning any data?
98: The usual causes are a page that loads its content with JavaScript, selectors that no longer match, or the site blocking the request. Re-run with rendering enabled, let AI Mode re-detect the fields, or route the run through the built-in proxies.
99: What’s the difference between AI Mode and Manual Mode?
100: AI Mode reads the page and extracts the fields you describe in plain language - the fastest way to a working scraper. Manual Mode gives you exact control with your own selectors and spends fewer tokens on predictable, high-volume runs.
101: When should I use a proxy?
102: Use one when a site limits how often one address can visit, or serves different content per country. Location-based proxies let you see each page as it appears in the region you choose.
103: Does MrScraper provide built-in proxies?
104: Yes. Residential proxies with country-level targeting are built into the platform - enable them per scraper, with no third-party setup. Bandwidth is billed separately from plan tokens, from $1.5/GB.
105: Can I schedule scrapers to run automatically?
106: Yes. Any scraper can run on a schedule, from once a minute to specific days of the week, and each run can deliver its results onward automatically.
107: Can I use MrScraper to track product reviews or sentiment?
108: Yes. Point a scraper at product or review pages and extract ratings, review text, and dates into structured rows, then schedule it so the dataset stays fresh for sentiment analysis.
109: How can I extract job listings with specific criteria?
110: Scrape the job board’s search or listing pages and describe the fields you need - title, company, location, salary. Filters in the target URL carry over, so the scraper only collects listings that match your criteria.
111: How can I lower my scraping costs?
112: Tokens are charged on the data a scrape extracts, so collect only the fields you need, prefer Manual Mode for stable high-volume jobs, and schedule runs at the frequency the data actually changes.
113: Can MrScraper send my data automatically?
114: Yes. Results can go straight to webhooks, SQL databases, AWS S3, Zapier, n8n, or email, so scraped data lands in your workflow without manual exports.
115: Why do some runs fail or hit rate limits?
116: Some sites limit how often they can be visited, and some only show their content once JavaScript has run. Enable the built-in residential proxies, lower the run frequency, and let the browser render the full page - most failed runs clear up with those three.
117: My scheduled scrapes didn’t run - what can I check?
118: Check that the schedule is still enabled, your token balance isn't exhausted (extra usage is $1 per 1,000 tokens), and the target page still matches the scraper's setup. The run history shows each attempt's result - if it still looks wrong, contact support from the dashboard.
119: Couldn't find your answer? Contact our team for a quick support.
120: Meet MrScraper, a visual web scraper to extract data from public websites, easily and reliably.

69: # Apify API
70: The Apify API (version 2) provides programmatic access to the [Apify platform](https://docs.apify.com). The API is organized around [RESTful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representational_state_transfer) HTTP endpoints.
71: You can download the complete OpenAPI schema of Apify API in the [YAML](http://docs.apify.com/api/openapi.yaml) or [JSON](http://docs.apify.com/api/openapi.json) formats. The source code is also available on [GitHub](https://github.com/apify/apify-docs/tree/master/apify-api/openapi).
72: All requests and responses (including errors) are encoded in [JSON](http://www.json.org/) format with UTF-8 encoding, with a few exceptions that are explicitly described in the reference.
73: To access the API, we recommend using one of our API clients:
74: Stable API clients:
75: * For [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/), we recommend the [apify-client](https://docs.apify.com/api/client/js) [NPM package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/apify-client).
76: * For [Python](https://www.python.org/), we recommend the [apify-client](https://docs.apify.com/api/client/python) [PyPI package](https://pypi.org/project/apify-client/).
77: Experimental API clients:
78: * For [Java](https://www.java.com/), we recommend the `apify-client` [Maven central component](https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/com.apify/apify-client).
79: * For [Rust](https://rust-lang.org/), we recommend the `apify-client` [crate](https://crates.io/crates/apify-client).
80: * For [.NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/), we recommend the `apify-client` [Nuget package](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Apify.Client).
81: * For [PHP](https://www.php.net/), we recommend the `apify-client` [Packagist package](https://packagist.org/packages/apify/apify-client).
82: * For [Go](https://go.dev/), we recommend the `apify-client` [package](https://github.com/apify/apify-client-go/releases).
83: The clients' functions correspond to the API endpoints and have the same parameters. This simplifies development of apps that depend on the Apify platform.
84: Important Request Details
85: * `Content-Type` header: For requests with a JSON body, you must include the `Content-Type: application/json` header.
86: * Method override: You can override the HTTP method using the `method` query parameter. This is useful for clients that can only send `GET` requests. For example, to call a `POST` endpoint, append `?method=POST` to the URL of your `GET` request.
87: ## Authentication
88: **You can create an API token on the [Integrations](https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations) page in the Apify Console.** The Console shows the token only once, right after you create or rotate it, so copy it and store it somewhere safe. For details, see [API token](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/api#api-token).
89: To use your token in a request, either:
90: * *(Recommended)* Add the token to your request's `Authorization` header as `Bearer <token>`. E.g., `Authorization: Bearer xxxxxxx`. For details, see the [Authorization header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Authorization) on MDN.
91: * Add it as the `token` parameter to your request URL. (Less secure).
92: Using your token in the request header is more secure than using it as a URL parameter because URLs are often stored in browser history and server logs. This creates a chance for someone unauthorized to access your API token.
93: **Never share your API token or password with untrusted parties!**
94: For more information, see our [integrations](https://docs.apify.com/platform/integrations) documentation.
95: ### Agentic payments
96: AI agents can authenticate and pay for Actor runs without an Apify account using agentic payments. Instead of an API token, the request carries a payment credential that both authorizes and pays for the call. Apify supports the [x402 protocol](https://docs.apify.com/platform/integrations/x402) (`PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header) and [Skyfire](https://docs.apify.com/platform/integrations/skyfire) (`skyfire-pay-id` header).
97: Agents can also pay once with x402 or the [Machine Payments Protocol (MPP)](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/mpp) and receive a temporary API token with a fixed spend cap from the Apify Agent General Interface (AGI) at [https://agi.apify.com](https://agi.apify.com). Use that token as a regular `Bearer` token.
98: ## Basic usage
99: To run an Actor, send a POST request to the [Run Actor](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actors-runs-post.md) endpoint using either the Actor ID code (e.g. `vKg4IjxZbEYTYeW8T`) or its name (e.g. `janedoe~my-actor`):
100: `https://api.apify.com/v2/actors/[actor_id]/runs`
101: If the Actor is not runnable anonymously, you will receive a 401 or 403 [response code](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status). This means you need to add your [secret API token](https://console.apify.com/account#/integrations) to the request's `Authorization` header (recommended) or as a URL query parameter `?token=[your_token]` (less secure).
102: Optionally, you can include the query parameters described in the [Run Actor](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actors-runs-post.md) section to customize your run.
103: If you're using Node.js, the best way to run an Actor is using the `Apify.call()` method from the [Apify SDK](https://sdk.apify.com/docs/api/apify#apifycallactid-input-options). It runs the Actor using the account you are currently logged into (determined by the [secret API token](https://console.apify.com/account#/integrations)). The result is an [Actor run object](https://sdk.apify.com/docs/typedefs/actor-run) and its output (if any).
104: A typical workflow is as follows:
105: 1. Run an Actor or task using the [Run Actor](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actors-runs-post.md) or [Run Actor task](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-task-runs-post.md) API endpoints.
106: 2. Monitor the Actor run by periodically polling its progress using the [Get Actor run](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-run-get.md) API endpoint.
107: 3. Fetch the results from the [Get dataset items](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/dataset-items-get.md) API endpoint using the `defaultDatasetId`, which you receive in the Run request response. Additional data may be stored in a key-value store. You can fetch them from the [Get key-value store record](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-record-get.md) API endpoint using the `defaultKeyValueStoreId` and the store's `key`.
108: **Note**: Instead of periodic polling, you can also run your Actor or task synchronously with the [Run Actor synchronously and get key-value store record](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-run-sync-post.md) or [Run Actor task synchronously and get key-value store record](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-task-run-sync-post.md) endpoint. This will ensure that the request waits for 300 seconds (5 minutes) for the run to finish and returns its output. If the run takes longer, the request will time out and throw an error.
109: ## Legacy `/v2/acts/` URL prefix
110: The `/v2/acts/` prefix is deprecated but still fully functional, and such endpoint routes to the same handler as its `/v2/actors/...` counterpart. New integrations should use the canonical /v2/actors/ prefix, but existing clients keep working without changes.
111: ## Response structure
112: Most API endpoints return a JSON object with the `data` property:
113: ```typescript
114: {
115: "data": {
116: ...
117: }
118: }
119: ```
120: However, there are a few explicitly described exceptions, such as [Get dataset items](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/dataset-items-get.md) or [Get key-value store record](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-record-get.md) API endpoints, which return data in other formats. In case of an error, the response has the HTTP status code in the range of 4xx or 5xx and the `data` property is replaced with `error`. For example:
121: ```typescript
122: {
123: "error": {
124: "type": "record-not-found",
125: "message": "Store was not found."
126: }
127: }
128: ```
129: See Errors for more details.
130: ## Pagination
131: All API endpoints that return a list of records (e.g. [Get list of Actors](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actors-get.md)) enforce pagination in order to limit the size of their responses.
132: Most of these API endpoints are paginated using the `offset` and `limit` query parameters. The only exception is [Get list of key-value store keys](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-keys-get.md), which is paginated using the `exclusiveStartKey` query parameter.
133: **IMPORTANT**: Each API endpoint that supports pagination enforces a certain maximum value for the `limit` parameter, in order to reduce the load on Apify servers. The maximum limit could change in future so you should never rely on a specific value and check the responses of these API endpoints.
134: ### Using offset
135: Most API endpoints that return a list of records enable pagination using the following query parameters:
136: | | |
137: | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
138: | `limit` | Limits the response to contain a specific maximum number of items, e.g. `limit=20`. |
139: | `offset` | Skips a number of items from the beginning of the list, e.g. `offset=100`. |
140: | `desc` | By default, items are sorted in the order in which they were created or added to the list. This feature is useful when fetching all the items, because it ensures that items created after the client started the pagination will not be skipped. If you specify the `desc=1` parameter, the items will be returned in the reverse order, i.e. from the newest to the oldest items. |
141: The response of these API endpoints is always a JSON object with the following structure:
142: ```typescript
143: {
144: "data": {
145: "total": 2560,
146: "offset": 250,
147: "limit": 1000,
148: "count": 1000,
149: "desc": false,
150: "items": [
151: { 1st object },
152: { 2nd object },
153: ...
154: { 1000th object }
155: ]
156: }
157: }
158: ```
159: The following table describes the meaning of the response properties:
160: | Property | Description |
161: | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
162: | `total` | The total number of items available in the list. |
163: | `offset` | The number of items that were skipped at the start. This is equal to the `offset` query parameter if it was provided, otherwise it is `0`. |
164: | `limit` | The maximum number of items that can be returned in the HTTP response. It equals to the `limit` query parameter if it was provided or the maximum limit enforced for the particular API endpoint, whichever is smaller. |
165: | `count` | The actual number of items returned in the HTTP response. |
166: | `desc` | `true` if data were requested in descending order and `false` otherwise. |
167: | `items` | An array of requested items. |
168: ### Using key
169: The records in the [key-value store](https://docs.apify.com/platform/storage/key-value-store) are not ordered based on numerical indexes, but rather by their keys in the UTF-8 binary order. Therefore the [Get list of key-value store keys](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-keys-get.md) API endpoint only supports pagination using the following query parameters:
170: | | |
171: | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
172: | `limit` | Limits the response to contain a specific maximum number items, e.g. `limit=20`. |
173: | `exclusiveStartKey` | Skips all records with keys up to the given key including the given key, in the UTF-8 binary order. |
174: The response of the API endpoint is always a JSON object with following structure:
175: ```typescript
176: {
177: "data": {
178: "limit": 1000,
179: "isTruncated": true,
180: "exclusiveStartKey": "my-key",
181: "nextExclusiveStartKey": "some-other-key",
182: "items": [
183: { 1st object },
184: { 2nd object },
185: ...
186: { 1000th object }
187: ]
188: }
189: }
190: ```
191: The following table describes the meaning of the response properties:
192: | Property | Description |
193: | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
194: | `limit` | The maximum number of items that can be returned in the HTTP response. It equals to the `limit` query parameter if it was provided or the maximum limit enforced for the particular endpoint, whichever is smaller. |
195: | `isTruncated` | `true` if there are more items left to be queried. Otherwise `false`. |
196: | `exclusiveStartKey` | The last key that was skipped at the start. Is `null` for the first page. |
197: | `nextExclusiveStartKey` | The value for the `exclusiveStartKey` parameter to query the next page of items. |
198: ## Errors
199: The Apify API uses common HTTP status codes: 2xx range for success, 4xx range for errors caused by the caller (invalid requests) and 5xx range for server errors (these are rare). Each error response contains a JSON object defining the `error` property, which is an object with the `type` and `message` properties that contain the error code and a human-readable error description, respectively.
200: For example:
201: ```typescript
202: {
203: "error": {
204: "type": "record-not-found",
205: "message": "Store was not found."
206: }
207: }
208: ```
209: Here is the table of the most common errors that can occur for many API endpoints:
210: | status | type | message |
211: | ------ | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
212: | 400 | `invalid-request` | POST data must be a JSON object |
213: | 400 | `invalid-value` | Invalid value provided: Comments required |
214: | 400 | `invalid-record-key` | Record key contains invalid character |
215: | 401 | `token-not-provided` | Authentication token was not provided |
216: | 404 | `record-not-found` | Store was not found |
217: | 429 | `rate-limit-exceeded` | You have exceeded the rate limit of ... requests per second |
218: | 405 | `method-not-allowed` | This API endpoint can only be accessed using the following HTTP methods: OPTIONS, POST |
219: ## Rate limiting
220: All API endpoints limit the rate of requests in order to prevent overloading of Apify servers by misbehaving clients.
221: There are two kinds of rate limits - a global rate limit and a per-resource rate limit.
222: ### Global rate limit
223: The global rate limit is set to *250 000 requests per minute*. For authenticated requests, it is counted per user, and for unauthenticated requests, it is counted per IP address.
224: ### Per-resource rate limit
225: The default per-resource rate limit is *60 requests per second per resource*, which in this context means a single Actor, a single Actor run, a single dataset, single key-value store etc. The default rate limit is applied to every API endpoint except a few select ones, which have higher rate limits. Each API endpoint returns its rate limit in `X-RateLimit-Limit` header.
226: These endpoints have a rate limit of *35 requests per second per resource*:
227: * [Batch add requests to request queue](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-requests-batch-post.md)
228: * [Batch delete requests from request queue](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-requests-batch-delete.md)
229: * [Get and lock request queue head](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-head-lock-post.md)
230: These endpoints have a rate limit of *100 requests per second per resource*:
231: * [Download key-value store records](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-records-get.md) (ZIP archive)
232: These endpoints have a rate limit of *200 requests per second per resource*:
233: * [Get key-value store record](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-record-get.md)
234: * [Set key-value store record](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-record-put.md) and its [POST variant](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-record-post.md)
235: * [Delete key-value store record](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-record-delete.md)
236: * [Get list of key-value store keys](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-keys-get.md)
237: These endpoints have a rate limit of *350 requests per second per resource*:
238: * [Add request to request queue](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-requests-post.md)
239: * [Get request from request queue](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-request-get.md)
240: * [Update request in request queue](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-request-put.md)
241: * [Delete request from request queue](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-request-delete.md)
242: * [Prolong lock on request in request queue](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-request-lock-put.md)
243: * [Delete lock on request in request queue](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/request-queue-request-lock-delete.md)
244: These endpoints have a rate limit of *400 requests per second per resource*:
245: * [Run Actor](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actors-runs-post.md)
246: * [Run Actor task](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-task-runs-post.md)
247: * [Run Actor task synchronously and get key-value store record](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-task-run-sync-post.md) and its [GET variant](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-task-run-sync-get.md)
248: * [Run Actor task synchronously and get dataset items](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-task-run-sync-get-dataset-items-post.md) and its [GET variant](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-task-run-sync-get-dataset-items-get.md)
249: * [Metamorph Actor run](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/actor-run-metamorph-post.md)
250: * [Store items in dataset](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/dataset-items-post.md)
251: ### Rate limit exceeded errors
252: If the client is sending too many requests, the API endpoints respond with the HTTP status code `429 Too Many Requests` and the following body:
253: ```typescript
254: {
255: "error": {
256: "type": "rate-limit-exceeded",
257: "message": "You have exceeded the rate limit of ... requests per second"
258: }
259: }
260: ```
261: ### Retrying rate-limited requests with exponential backoff
262: If the client receives the rate limit error, it should wait a certain period of time and then retry the request. If the error happens again, the client should double the wait period and retry the request, and so on. This algorithm is known as *exponential backoff* and it can be described using the following pseudo-code:
263: 1. Define a variable `DELAY=500`
264: 2. Send the HTTP request to the API endpoint
265: 3. If the response has status code not equal to 429 then you are done. Otherwise:
266: <!-- -->
267: * Wait for a period of time chosen randomly from the interval `DELAY` to `2*DELAY` milliseconds
268: * Double the future wait period by setting `DELAY = 2*DELAY`
269: * Continue with step 2
270: If all requests sent by the client implement the above steps, the client will automatically use the maximum available bandwidth for its requests.
271: Note that the Apify API clients [for JavaScript](https://docs.apify.com/api/client/js) and [for Python](https://docs.apify.com/api/client/python) use the exponential backoff algorithm transparently, so that you do not need to worry about it.
272: ## Referring to resources
273: There are three main ways to refer to a resource you're accessing via API.
274: * the resource ID (e.g. `iKkPcIgVvwmztduf8`)
275: * `username~resourcename` - when using this access method, you will need to use your API token, and access will only work if you have the correct permissions.
276: * `~resourcename` - for this, you need to use an API token, and the `resourcename` refers to a resource in the API token owner's account.
277: ## Authentication
278: * HTTP: Bearer Auth
279: * API Key: apiKey
280: Bearer token provided in the `Authorization` header (e.g., `Authorization: Bearer your_token`—recommended). For details, see the [Authorization header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Authorization) on MDN.
281: Use your API token to authenticate requests. You can create one on the [Integrations page](https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations) in Apify Console. The Console shows the token only once, right after you create or rotate it, so copy it and store it somewhere safe. This method is more secure than query parameters, as headers are not logged in browser history or server logs.
282: Security
283: Do not share your API token (or account password) with untrusted parties.
284: *When is authentication required?*
285: * *Required* for private Actors, tasks, or resources (e.g., builds of private Actors).
286: * *Required* when using named formats for IDs (e.g., `username~store-name` for stores or `username~queue-name` for queues).
287: * *Optional* for public Actors or resources (e.g., builds of public Actors can be queried without a token).
288: For more information, see our [integrations documentation](https://docs.apify.com/platform/integrations).
289: | Security Scheme Type: | http |
290: | -------------------------- | ------ |
291: | HTTP Authorization Scheme: | bearer |
292: API token provided as a query parameter (e.g., `?token=your_token`—less secure).
293: Use your API token to authenticate requests. You can create one on the [Integrations page](https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations) in Apify Console. The Console shows the token only once, right after you create or rotate it, so copy it and store it somewhere safe.
294: Security
295: Do not share your API token (or account password) with untrusted parties.
296: *When is authentication required?*
297: * *Required* for private Actors, tasks, or resources (e.g., builds of private Actors).
298: * *Required* when using named formats for IDs (e.g., `username~store-name` for stores or `username~queue-name` for queues).
299: * *Optional* for public Actors or resources (e.g., builds of public Actors can be queried without a token).
300: For more information, see our [integrations documentation](https://docs.apify.com/platform/integrations).
301: | Security Scheme Type: | apiKey |
302: | --------------------- | ------ |
303: | Query parameter name: | token |

11: > ## Documentation index
12: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.apify.com/llms.txt
13: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
14: # API integration
15: All aspects of the Apify platform can be controlled via a REST API, which is described in detail in the [API Reference](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2.md). If you want to use the Apify API from JavaScript/Node.js or Python, we strongly recommend using one of the API clients:
16: * [apify-client](https://docs.apify.com/api/client/js) `npm` package for JavaScript, supporting both browser and server
17: * [apify-client](https://docs.apify.com/api/client/python) PyPI package for Python.
18: You are not required to those packages - the REST API works with any HTTP client - but the official API clients implement best practices such as exponential backoff and rate limiting.
19: ## API token
20: To access the Apify API in your integrations, you need to authenticate using your secret API token. You manage your tokens on the [API & Integrations](https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations) page in Apify Console. Give each token a reasonable description, and never use one token for several services, much like you shouldn't use the same password for different accounts.
21: Apify Console shows the value of an API token only once, right after you create or rotate it. The token list shows each token's description, a masked preview of its value, when it was last used, and when it expires, but you can't view or copy the full value of an existing token.
22: The Apify CLI doesn't need a copied token. When you sign in with [apify login](https://docs.apify.com/cli/docs/reference#apify-auth-login--apify-login) in the browser, it creates a token for your device and stores it for you.
23: Protect your API token
24: Do not share the API token with untrusted parties, or use it directly from client-side code, unless you fully understand the consequences! You can also consider limiting the permission scope of the token, so that it can only access what it really needs.
25: ### Create an API token
26: 1. Go to [Settings > API & Integrations](https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations) in Apify Console.
27: 2. In the **Personal API tokens** section, select **Create a new token**.
28: 3. Enter a description. Optionally, limit the token's permissions or set an expiration date.
29: 4. Select **Create**.
30: 5. Copy the token and store it somewhere safe, such as a password manager.
31: 6. Select **Done**.
32: If you lose a token, rotate it to get a new value, or create a new token and delete the old one.
33: ## Authentication
34: You can authenticate the Apify API in two ways. You can either pass the token via the `Authorization` HTTP header or the URL `token` query parameter. We always recommend you use the authentication via the HTTP header as this method is more secure.
35: Note that some API endpoints, such as [Get list of key-value store keys](https://docs.apify.com/api/v2/key-value-store-keys-get.md), do not require an authentication token because they contain a hard-to-guess identifier that effectively serves as an authentication key.
36: ## Expiration
37: API tokens include security features to protect your account and data. You can set an expiration date for your API tokens, ensuring they become invalid after a specified period. This is particularly useful for temporary access or when working with third-party services.
38: ![Creating token with expiration date in Apify Console](/assets/images/api-token-expiration-date-422b4f0433871dbeee59a23d06010f21.png)
39: ## Rotation
40: If you suspect that a token has been compromised or accidentally exposed, you can rotate it through Apify Console. When rotating a token, you have the option to keep the old token active for 24 hours, allowing you to update your applications with the new token before the old one becomes invalid. After the rotation period, the token will be regenerated, and any applications connected to the old token will need to be updated with the new token to continue functioning.
41: ![Rotate token in Apify Console](/assets/images/api-token-rotate-6c21e1e4fc3f5507882868822a71b6a4.png)
42: After you confirm the rotation, Apify Console shows the new token. This is the only time you can copy it, so store it somewhere safe.
43: For better security awareness, the UI marks tokens identified as compromised with a **Leaked** label, making it easy to identify and take action on them.
44: ## Organization accounts
45: When working under an organization account, you will see two types of API tokens on the API & Integrations page.
46: The Personal API tokens are different from your own Personal API tokens mentioned above. If you use this token in an integration, it will have the same permissions that you have within the organization, and all the operations you use it for will be ascribed to you.
47: On the other hand the Organization API tokens (only visible if you are the owner or have Manage access tokens permission) have full permissions and are not tied to a specific member of the organization.
48: ## API tokens with limited permissions
49: By default, tokens can access all data in your account. If that is not desirable, you can choose to limit the permissions of your token, so that it can only access data needed for the particular use case. We call these tokens **scoped**.
50: **A scoped token can access only those resources that you'll explicitly allow it to.**
51: Actor modification restrictions
52: We do not allow scoped tokens to create or modify Actors. If you do need to create or modify Actors through the Apify API, use an unscoped token.
53: ### How to create a scoped token
54: Scoped tokens behave like standard API tokens and are managed through the [API & Integrations](https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations) page in Apify Console. When creating a token (or updating an existing one), simply toggle "Limit token permissions" to make the token scoped.
55: Once the token is scoped, you can specify the token's permissions.
56: ![Toggle \"Limit token permissions\" to make a token scoped](/assets/images/api-token-scoped-1924cb0bcb243160c2c0e3db9d7e31b8.png)
57: ### Account-level vs resource-specific permissions
58: We support two different types of permissions for tokens:
59: * **Account-level permissions**: These will apply to all resources in the entire account. For example, you can use these to allow the token to run *all* your Actors.
60: * **Resource-specific permissions**: These will apply only to specific, existing resources. For example, you can use these to allow the token to read from a particular dataset.
61: Combine permission types
62: A single token can combine both types. You can create a token that can *read* any data storage, but *write* only to one specific key-value store.
63: ![An example scoped token that combines account-level permissions and resource-specific permissions](/assets/images/api-token-scoped-with-combining-permissions-2a215b511b0705b7617fe154df80ed15.png)
64: ### Allow tokens to create resources
65: If you need to create new resources with the token (for example, create a new task, or storage), you need to explicitly allow that as well.
66: Once you create a new resource with the token, *the token will gain full access to that resource*, regardless of other permissions. It is not possible to create a token that can create a dataset, but not write to it.
67: Dynamic resource creation
68: This is useful if you want to for example create a token that can dynamically create & populate datasets, but without the need to access other datasets in your account.
69: ### Permission dependencies
70: Some permissions require other permissions to be granted alongside them. These are called *permission dependencies*.
71: #### Automatic dependencies
72: The form enforces certain dependencies automatically. For example, when you grant the **Write** permission for a dataset, the **Read** permission is automatically selected. This ensures that when you can write to a dataset you can also read from it.
73: ![The Write permission depends on Read for a dataset](/assets/images/api-token-scoped-dependencies-0af67b93c684001175ddc3f273eff652.png)
74: #### Manual dependencies
75: Other dependencies are more complicated, so it is up to you to ensure that the token is configured correctly.
76: Specifically:
77: * To create or update a Schedule, the token needs access not only to the Schedule itself, but also to the Actor (the **Run** permission) or task (the **Read** permission) that is being scheduled.
78: * Similarly, to create, update or run a task, the token needs the **Run** permission on the task's Actor itself.
79: Schedule creation example
80: Let's say that you have an Actor and you want to programmatically create schedules for that Actor. Then you can create a token that has the account level **Create** permission on schedules, but only the resource-specific **Run** permission on the Actor. Such a token has exactly the permissions it needs, and nothing more.
81: ### Actor execution
82: When you run an Actor, Apify creates a new, short-lived run API token, and injects it into the Actor environment. This applies to scoped tokens as well, so when you run an Actor with a scoped token, **the Actor is executed with a different token with a different scope.**
83: In the scoped token configuration you can choose what scope the run API token gets, effectively determining what the Actor can access during its run.
84: Apify currently supports two modes:
85: * **Full access**: Allow Actors to access all your account's data.
86: * **Restricted access**: Restrict what Actors can access using the scope of this Actor.
87: ![Choose permission mode for running Actors with a scoped token](/assets/images/api-token-scoped-run-modes-7d0d9163f379ea085781f96e34295844.png)
88: #### Full access: Allow Actors to access all your account's data
89: When you run an Actor with a scoped token in this mode, Apify will inject an *unscoped* token to the Actor runtime.
90: This way you can be sure that once you give a token the permission to run an Actor, it will just work, and you don't have to worry about the exact permissions the Actor might need. However, this also means that you need to trust the Actor.
91: Third-party integration
92: Use this mode if you want to integrate with a 3rd-party service to run your Actors. Create a scoped token that can only run the Actor you need, and share it with the service. Even if the token is leaked, it can't be used to access your other data.
93: #### Restricted access: Restrict what Actors can access using the scope of this Actor
94: When you run an Actor with a scoped token in this mode, Apify will inject a token with the same scope as the scope of the original token.
95: This way you can be sure that Actors won't accidentally - or intentionally - access any data they shouldn't. However, Actors might not function properly if the scope is not sufficient.
96: Server Actors limitation
97: Restricted access mode is not supported for [Server Actors](https://docs.apify.com/actors/running/server-actors.md). While you can send requests to Server Actors using a scoped token configured with restricted access, functionality is not guaranteed.
98: Transitive restrictions
99: This restriction is *transitive*, which means that if the Actor runs another Actor, its access will be restricted as well.
100: #### Default run storages
101: When Apify [runs an Actor](https://docs.apify.com/actors/running/runs-and-builds.md#runs), it automatically creates a set of default storages (a dataset, a key-value store and request queue) that the Actor can use in runtime.
102: You can configure whether the scoped token you are going use to run the Actor should get access to these default storages.
103: ![Configure whether the trigger token gets write access to the run default storages.](/assets/images/api-token-scoped-default-storage-access-5b35df1f6168356aeb9029192f9572e8.png)
104: If it’s **on**, the token can implicitly access the default storage of the Actor runs it triggers, or in general, of any Actor run in your account that falls within its scope. This is useful if you want to allow a third-party service to run an Actor and then read the Actor’s output (think AI agents).
105: If the toggle is **off**, the token can still trigger and inspect runs, but access to the default storages is restricted:
106: * For accounts with **Restricted general resource access**, the token cannot read or write to default storages. [Learn more about restricted general resource access](https://docs.apify.com/account/collaboration/general-resource-access.md).
107: * For accounts with **Unrestricted general resource access**, the default storages can still be read anonymously using their IDs, but writing is prevented.
108: Clean up run data
109: Let's say your Actor produces a lot of data that you want to delete just after the Actor finishes. If you enable this toggle, your scoped token will be allowed to do that.
110: ### Schedules
111: You can use scoped tokens to schedule Actor and Tasks. Each schedule invocation triggers a new Actor run, creating and injecting a new run API token into the Actor.
112: However, **this token is always unscoped, which means that the scheduled Actor has access to all your account data**, regardless of the scope of the token that scheduled it.
113: ### Webhooks configuration
114: If you allow a token to run an Actor, it'll also be able to manage the Actor's webhooks (similarly for tasks).
115: If you set up a webhook pointing to the Apify API, the Apify platform will automatically inject a token when dispatching that webhook. However, if you set up such a webhook with a scoped token, **that webhook will be dispatched with a token with the same limited permissions**.
116: Therefore, you need to make sure the token has sufficient permissions not only to set up the webhook, but also to perform the actual operation.
117: Webhook permissions
118: Let's say you want to create a webhook that pushes an item to a dataset every time an Actor successfully finishes. Then such a scoped token needs to be allowed to both run the Actor (to create the webhook), and write to that dataset.
119: ### Troubleshooting
120: #### How do I allow a token to run a task?
121: Tasks don't have a dedicated **Run** permission. Instead, you should configure the token with the following permissions:
122: * **Run** on the Actor that the task is executing
123: * **Read** on the task
124: See the following example:
125: ![Scoped token configured to run a task](/assets/images/api-token-scoped-run-tasks-ef961ddca69d18ff3797ee47ccafe44e.png)
126: Refer to this section to understand how permission dependencies work.
127: #### My run failed and I can see `insufficient permissions` in the logs
128: When a run fails with insufficient permissions in the logs, it typically means the Actor is using a scoped token with **Restricted access** configured.
129: ![Scoped token with Restricted access](/assets/images/api-token-scoped-restricted-access-active-bdd6f312a8bf9ea7e8dfbe2e31c3df60.png)
130: What is happening is that the Actor is trying to access a resource (such as a dataset, or a key-value store) or perform an operation that it does not have sufficient permissions for.
131: If you know what it is, you can add the permission to the scope of your token. If you don't, you can switch the permission mode on the token to **Full access**. This means that the Actor will be able to access all your account data.
132: Refer to Actor execution section to understand how executing Actors with scoped tokens works.
