8: ---
9: > ## Documentation index
10: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.apify.com/llms.txt
11: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
12: # Apify MCP server
13: The Apify's MCP server ([mcp.apify.com](https://mcp.apify.com)) allows AI applications and agents to interact with the Apify platform using [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro) (MCP). The MCP server enables AI agents to discover and run Actors from [Apify Store](https://apify.com/store), access storages and results, and enables AI coding assistants to access Apify documentation and tutorials.
14: To connect a coding agent such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, or Codex, install the [Apify plugin](https://docs.apify.com/agents/plugins.md) instead. It sets up this server together with [Agent Skills](https://docs.apify.com/agents/skills.md) in one step.
15: ![Apify MCP server](/assets/images/apify_mcp_server-d7b7369162651886da809d991d23e26e.png)
16: Apify MCP server vs MCP connectors
17: This page covers the Apify MCP server, which exposes Apify Actors as tools to outside AI clients. If you are building an Actor that needs to call third-party MCP servers (such as Notion or Slack) on a user's behalf, see [MCP connectors](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/mcp-connectors.md) instead.
18: ## Apify AI vs the MCP server
19: The Apify MCP server and [Apify AI](https://docs.apify.com/account/apify-ai.md) share the same Actor search and execution backend, but they serve different audiences:
20: * *MCP server* - a programmatic interface for external AI agents, IDEs, and CLIs. Use it when you build or operate your own agent.
21: * *Apify AI* - the conversational interface inside [Apify Console](https://console.apify.com) for users who interact with Apify through a chat UI rather than their own agent.
22: Actor ranking on both surfaces uses parameters similar to those evaluated by the [Actor quality score](https://docs.apify.com/actors/publishing/quality-score.md), so Actors with higher quality scores tend to rank higher.
23: ## Excluded Actors
24: Due to security reasons, the MCP server intentionally excludes full-permission Actors from search and execution. Running a [full-permission Actor](https://docs.apify.com/actors/running/permissions.md#full-permission-actors) is a decision you approve personally, so an LLM can't make it on your behalf.
25: ## Prerequisites
26: Before connecting your AI to Apify, you need:
27: * *An Apify account* - You need one unless your agent uses only the tools that work without an account or pays through agentic payments. Sign up for an Apify account, if you don't have one.
28: * *MCP client* - An AI agent or client that supports Model Context Protocol (MCP). This could be [claude.ai](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/claude-ai.md), [Claude Desktop](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/claude-desktop.md), [VS Code](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/vscode.md) with MCP support, or any application that implements the MCP specification. The [official MCP documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/clients) maintains a list of compatible clients.
29: * *Apify API token* (optional) - Only needed for the local stdio server or the Bearer token option. The recommended remote connection signs you in with OAuth instead. [Create an API token](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/api.md#create-api-token) in Apify Console.
30: ## Connect and authorize
31: To discover Actors and search the documentation, you can connect without an account. To run Actors, connect in one of two ways: use the hosted Apify service with Streamable HTTP with OAuth, or run the server locally for development and testing with local stdio.
32: Structured output schemas
33: The hosted Apify MCP server at `https://mcp.apify.com` supports *output schema inference* for structured Actor results. Actor tools automatically include inferred output schemas with field-level type information. This helps AI agents understand the expected result structure before calling an Actor. The local stdio server does not support this feature.
34: ### Use without an account
35: The Apify MCP server accepts requests without an API token when the `tools` query parameter (see Tool selection) contains only tools enabled for unauthenticated use. These tools cover Actor discovery, documentation lookup, and the Apify API reference:
36: * `search-actors`
37: * `fetch-actor-details`
38: * `search-apify-docs`
39: * `fetch-apify-docs`
40: * `apify-api-search`
41: * `apify-api-details`
42: For example, the following URL connects without authentication:
43: `https://mcp.apify.com?tools=search-actors,fetch-actor-details,search-apify-docs,fetch-apify-docs`
44: If the `tools` parameter includes any other tool, or you connect to the default endpoint, the server requires an API token. Running Actors and accessing storage or run data always requires authentication, so use one of the methods below when you're ready to run Actors.
45: ### Streamable HTTP with OAuth (recommended)
46: Add `https://mcp.apify.com` to your MCP client. On first connection, your browser opens so you can sign in to Apify and approve access. To authorize without signing in, use your Apify API token instead.
47: **OAuth**
48: This flow authorizes the server without putting your API token in the client configuration.
49: ```json
50: {
51: "mcpServers": {
52: "apify": {
53: "url": "https://mcp.apify.com"
54: }
55: }
56: }
57: ```
58: **Bearer token**
59: You can also use your Apify token directly, instead of OAuth, by setting the `Authorization: Bearer <APIFY_TOKEN>` header in the MCP server configuration.
60: ```json
61: {
62: "mcpServers": {
63: "apify": {
64: "url": "https://mcp.apify.com",
65: "headers": {
66: "Authorization": "Bearer <APIFY_TOKEN>"
67: }
68: }
69: }
70: }
71: ```
72: Replace `<APIFY_TOKEN>` with your [Apify API token](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/api.md#create-api-token).
73: For a client-specific configuration, use the [MCP configurator](https://mcp.apify.com/): pick the Actors and tools you need, then copy the generated configuration into your client. If you use the [Apify CLI](https://docs.apify.com/cli), `apify mcp install <client>` writes the configuration for you, for example `apify mcp install cursor`.
74: ### Local stdio
75: If your client doesn't support remote MCP servers using the `https://mcp.apify.com` URL, you can run the server locally instead. This method uses the stdio transport to connect directly through your local environment.
76: Add this to your configuration file:
77: ```json
78: {
79: "mcpServers": {
80: "actors-mcp-server": {
81: "command": "npx",
82: "args": ["-y", "@apify/actors-mcp-server"],
83: "env": {
84: "APIFY_TOKEN": "YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN"
85: }
86: }
87: }
88: }
89: ```
90: The server will download automatically on first use and connect using your API token.
91: ## Agentic payments
92: Agents can pay for Actor runs without an Apify account. They buy a prepaid, spend-capped API token from [Apify AGI](https://agi.apify.com) and use it like a regular API token, so it runs any Actor that uses [limited permissions](https://docs.apify.com/actors/development/permissions.md).
93: Pass the token to the MCP server in the `Authorization` header:
94: ```json
95: {
96: "mcpServers": {
97: "apify": {
98: "url": "https://mcp.apify.com",
99: "headers": {
100: "Authorization": "Bearer <PREPAID_TOKEN>"
101: }
102: }
103: }
104: }
105: ```
106: For supported payment protocols and spending limits, read [Agentic payments](https://docs.apify.com/agents/payments.md).
107: ## Tool selection
108: By default, the MCP server loads the `actors` and `docs` tool categories, the `apify/web-search` and `apify/web-fetch` Actors, and `report-problem`. To choose different tools, set the `tools` parameter in the server URL. The parameter replaces the default selection instead of adding to it, so list everything you want to load:
109: `https://mcp.apify.com?tools=actors,docs,apify/web-search,apify/web-fetch`
110: For instance, `https://mcp.apify.com?tools=storage` loads only the storage tools, without `search-actors` or `call-actor`. The default Actors don't belong to any category, so `?tools=actors,docs` also drops them.
111: For minimal setups where you only need specific Actors:
112: `https://mcp.apify.com?tools=apify/instagram-scraper,apify/google-search-scraper`
113: Each Actor you select with the `tools` parameter becomes a tool of its own, named `{username}--{actor-name}`. For example, the server exposes `apify/web-search` as `apify--web-search`. The server replaces dots in the username with `-dot-` and shortens names longer than 64 characters by adding a hash suffix to keep them unique.
114: This configuration approach works for both hosted and local setups. For the CLI version:
115: `npx @apify/actors-mcp-server --tools actors,docs,apify/web-scraper`
116: To select your tools visually, use the [MCP configurator](https://mcp.apify.com/), then copy the generated configuration to your client.
117: ### Available tools
118: | Tool name | Category | Enabled by default | Description |
119: | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
120: | `search-actors` | `actors` | ✅ | Search for Actors in Apify Store |
121: | `fetch-actor-details` | `actors` | ✅ | Retrieve detailed information about a specific Actor, including its input and output schema, README (summary when available, full otherwise), and pricing |
122: | `call-actor` | `actors` | ✅ | Run an Actor and wait up to `waitSecs` (0-45, default 30) for it to finish. Pass run limits (`memory`, `timeout`, `maxItems`, `maxTotalChargeUsd`) in `callOptions`, not in the Actor input. Returns the run status and storage IDs, not the results themselves |
123: | `fetch-actor-mcp-tool-list` | `actors` | ✅ | List the tools of an Actor that runs an MCP server, with their schemas, annotations, and metadata |
124: | `call-actor-mcp-tool` | `actors` | ✅ | Call one tool on an Actor's MCP server and return its result |
125: | `send-server-actor-request` | `actors` | ✅ | Send one HTTP request to a Server Actor's API, as documented by its API schema, and return the response |
126: | [apify/web-search](https://apify.com/apify/web-search) | Actor | ✅ | Search the web and return the results in the response, without starting an Actor run |
127: | [apify/web-fetch](https://apify.com/apify/web-fetch) | Actor | ✅ | Fetch one http(s) URL and return its full content, rendering JavaScript and bypassing anti-bot protection |
128: | [apify/rag-web-browser](https://apify.com/apify/rag-web-browser) | Actor | | Search the web and return the content of the top results |
129: | `search-apify-docs` | `docs` | ✅ | Search the Apify documentation for relevant pages |
130: | `fetch-apify-docs` | `docs` | ✅ | Fetch the full content of an Apify documentation page by its URL |
131: | `get-actor-run` | `runs` | | Get detailed information about a specific Actor run |
132: | `get-actor-run-list` | `runs` | | Get a list of an Actor's runs, filterable by status |
133: | `get-actor-run-log` | `runs` | | Retrieve the logs for a specific Actor run |
134: | `abort-actor-run` | `runs` | | Abort a running Actor run |
135: | `get-dataset` | `storage` | | Get metadata about a specific dataset |
136: | `get-dataset-items` | `storage` | | Retrieve items from a dataset with support for filtering and pagination |
137: | `get-dataset-schema` | `storage` | | Generate a JSON schema from dataset items |
138: | `get-key-value-store` | `storage` | | Get metadata about a specific key-value store |
139: | `get-key-value-store-keys` | `storage` | | List the keys within a specific key-value store |
140: | `get-key-value-store-record` | `storage` | | Get the value associated with a specific key in a key-value store |
141: | `get-dataset-list` | `storage` | | List all available datasets for the user |
142: | `get-key-value-store-list` | `storage` | | List all available key-value stores for the user |
143: | `get-actor-task` | `tasks` | | Get a saved Actor task, its publication state, and its public display configuration |
144: | `create-actor-task` | `tasks` | | Create a saved Actor task: a named, reusable Actor configuration |
145: | `update-actor-task` | `tasks` | | Update a task's input, run options, or the display configuration of its landing page |
146: | `publish-actor-task` | `tasks` | | Publish a task on its public landing page |
147: | `unpublish-actor-task` | `tasks` | | Unpublish a task from its public landing page |
148: | `create-schedule` | `schedules` | | Create a schedule that runs Actors and tasks on a cron cadence |
149: | `get-schedule` | `schedules` | | Get a schedule's cron expression, time zone, state, and next run |
150: | `update-schedule` | `schedules` | | Change a schedule's cron expression, time zone, state, or actions |
151: | `delete-schedule` | `schedules` | | Delete a schedule permanently |
152: | `get-actor-build` | `builds` | | Get the status of an Actor build |
153: | `get-actor-build-log` | `builds` | | Read the log of an Actor build |
154: | `get-actor-build-list` | `builds` | | List the account's builds, or one Actor's, in every status, newest first |
155: | `build-actor` | `builds` | | Build an Actor version and wait a bounded time for the build to finish |
156: | `get-actor-version` | `versions` | | Get an Actor version's file listing with hashes, plus the content of the files you ask for |
157: | `create-actor` | `versions` | | Create a private Actor in your account from files, optionally starting a build |
158: | `update-actor-version` | `versions` | | Write, edit, or delete files of an Actor version in one all-or-nothing write |
159: | `create-actor-version` | `versions` | | Add a version to an Actor, from files or as a copy of another version, optionally starting a build |
160: | `delete-actor-version` | `versions` | | Delete an Actor version. Its builds and their tags stay |
161: | `apify-api-search` | `api` | | Search the Apify API reference by keywords |
162: | `apify-api-details` | `api` | | Get the parameters and request body schema of the Apify API operations on a path |
163: | `apify-api-read` | `api` | | Send a `GET` request to an Apify API path. Refuses the synchronous run endpoints, which start a paid run |
164: | `apify-api-write` | `api` | | Send a `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE` request with a JSON body to any Apify API path |
165: | `get-actor-list` | none | | List the Actors you own and those shared with you, including private ones. Load it by name: `tools=get-actor-list` |
166: | `delete-actor` | none | | Delete an Actor from your account permanently. Load it by name: `tools=delete-actor` |
167: | `report-problem` | `dev` | ✅ | Report a problem with the MCP server to Apify |
168: The server withholds `report-problem` when you turn off telemetry, and doesn't load it by default for some MCP clients. If your client doesn't get it by default, add `report-problem` or the `dev` category to the `tools` parameter. It stays unavailable while telemetry is off.
169: Retrieving Actor results
170: `call-actor` returns the run's status and storage IDs, not its output. To read the results, use `get-dataset-items` with the `datasetId` from the run. It supports limit, offset, and field filtering.
171: Whenever `call-actor` or an Actor tool that starts a run, such as `apify--instagram-scraper`, is loaded, the server also adds `get-actor-run`, `get-dataset-items`, `get-key-value-store-record`, and `abort-actor-run`, even if you didn't select them. A default configuration therefore exposes them too.
172: #### Find and call any Actor on demand
173: Your AI can search Apify Store for relevant Actors using the `search-actors` tool, inspect Actor details to understand required inputs, and call any Actor by name using `call-actor` - without needing to pre-configure it. This means your AI can adapt to new tasks without manual configuration.
174: ## Telemetry
175: The MCP server collects telemetry data about tool calls and MCP clients to help Apify understand usage patterns and improve the service. Participation in this program is optional and you may opt out if you prefer not to share any information.
176: ### Data collection
177: All telemetry data is collected and stored securely. We do not collect any sensitive information such as conversations, arguments passed to tools, API tokens, or personal data.
178: The server collects anonymous information about tool usage, including:
179: * Basic information about used tools (calls, success/failure, duration)
180: * MCP client attributes (client name, version, capabilities)
181: By default, telemetry is *enabled* for all tool calls.
182: ### Opt out of telemetry
183: #### Remote server
184: For the remote server (`mcp.apify.com`), you can opt out of telemetry by adding the `telemetry-enabled=false` query parameter to the server URL:
185: ```text
186: https://mcp.apify.com?telemetry-enabled=false
187: ```
188: #### Local stdio server
189: For the local stdio server, opt out of telemetry using a CLI flag or an environment variable. When both the CLI flag and environment variable are set, the CLI flag takes precedence.
190: * *CLI flag*: set the `--telemetry-enabled` CLI flag to `false`:
191: ```bash
192: npx @apify/actors-mcp-server --telemetry-enabled=false
193: ```
194: * *Environment variable*: set the `TELEMETRY_ENABLED` environment variable to `false`:
195: ```bash
196: export TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false
197: npx @apify/actors-mcp-server
198: ```
199: ## Advanced usage
200: ### Production best practices
201: * For production deployments, explicitly specify which tools to load rather than relying on defaults. This ensures consistent behavior across updates:
202: `https://mcp.apify.com?tools=actors,docs,apify/web-search,apify/web-fetch`
203: * For a local stdio server, always use the latest version of the server by appending `@latest` to your npm commands.
204: * Monitor your API usage through Apify Console to stay within your plan limits.
205: ## Rate limits and performance
206: The Apify MCP server allows up to *20* requests per second per user. This limit applies to all operations including Actor runs, storage access, and documentation queries. If you exceed this limit, you'll receive a `429` response and should implement appropriate retry logic.
207: ## Troubleshooting
208: Claude Desktop issues
209: For Claude Desktop-specific troubleshooting (tools not loading, connection errors, corrupted cache), see [Claude Desktop troubleshooting](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/claude-desktop.md#troubleshooting).
210: ##### Authentication errors
211: * *Check your API token*: Verify that your Apify API token is correct. Apify Console doesn't show the value of an existing token, so if you're unsure, [rotate it](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/api.md#rotation) or [create a new one](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/api.md#create-api-token). Without a valid token, the server cannot start Actor runs.
212: * *Set environment variable for local development*: When running the MCP server locally, ensure you have set the `APIFY_TOKEN` environment variable.
213: ##### Local environment setup
214: * *Node.js version*: The MCP server needs the Node.js version listed in the `engines` field of its [package.json](https://github.com/apify/apify-mcp-server/blob/master/package.json). Run `node -v` to check your installed version.
215: * *Using the latest server version*: To ensure you have the latest features and bug fixes, use the latest version of the `@apify/actors-mcp-server` package. You can do this by appending `@latest` to the package name in your `npx` command or configuration file.
216: ##### Actor execution issues
217: * *No response or long delays*: Actor runs can take time to complete depending on their task. If you're experiencing long delays, check the Actor's logs in Apify Console. The logs will provide insight into the Actor's status and show if it's processing a long operation or has encountered an error.
218: ## Support and resources
219: The Apify MCP server is an open-source project. Report bugs, suggest features, or ask questions in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/apify/apify-mcp-server/issues).
220: If you find this project useful, please star it on [GitHub](https://github.com/apify/apify-mcp-server) to show your support!
221: To learn more about MCP and Apify integration:
222: * [Model Context Protocol specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) - Learn about the open standard on the official MCP website - understanding the protocol can help you build custom agents.
223: * [How to use MCP with Apify Actors](https://blog.apify.com/how-to-use-mcp/) - Learn how to expose over thousands of Apify Actors to AI agents with Claude and LangGraph, and configure MCP clients and servers.
224: * [Video tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BKu8H91uCTg) - Integrate thousands of Apify Actors and Agents with Claude.
225: * [Apify Tester MCP Client](https://apify.com/jiri.spilka/tester-mcp-client) - A specialized client Actor that you can run to simulate an AI agent in your browser. Useful for testing your setup with a chat UI.

1: # Apify Documentation
2: > Apify is the largest marketplace of tools for AI. Thousands of ready-made Actors to automate your business. Get real-time web data, track competitors, generate leads, analyze sentiment, and orchestrate your apps. Actors are created by a global community of builders earning over $1M every month. Apify takes care of infrastructure, billing, and distribution.
3: The entire content of Apify documentation is available in a single Markdown file at https://docs.apify.com/llms-full.txt
4: For pricing details, see https://apify.com/pricing.md
5: For autonomous AI agents, the Apify Agent General Interface (AGI) at https://agi.apify.com is the entry point to use and pay for the Apify platform and Actors through agentic payment protocols like x402 or MPP, without account setup or ongoing billing.
6: ## Apify API
7: - [Apify API documentation](https://docs.apify.com/api/llms.txt): Endpoints to manage Actors, runs, builds, tasks, datasets, key-value stores, request queues, schedules, webhooks, and your account.
8: ## Apify API client for JavaScript

14: - [Pagination](https://docs.apify.com/api/client/js/docs/concepts/pagination.md): Paginate through large result sets and use async iteration with the Apify API client for JavaScript.

19: ## Apify API client for Python

107: - [Billing](https://docs.apify.com/account/billing.md): View invoices, track current billing cycle usage, manage subscriptions and limits, and review historical usage from the Billings page in Console.
108: - [Apply a promo code](https://docs.apify.com/account/billing/promo-codes.md): Learn how to apply a promo code to your invoice.
109: - [Collaboration](https://docs.apify.com/account/collaboration.md): Learn how to collaborate with other users and manage permissions for organizations or private resources such as Actors, Actor runs, and storages.
110: - [Grant access rights](https://docs.apify.com/account/collaboration/access-rights.md): Manage permissions for your private resources such as Actors, Actor runs, and storages. Allow other users to read, run, modify, or build new versions.
111: - [General resource access](https://docs.apify.com/account/collaboration/general-resource-access.md): Control how Apify resources are shared. Set default access to open ID-based access or restricted, and manage link sharing and pre-signed URLs.
112: - [List of permissions](https://docs.apify.com/account/collaboration/list-of-permissions.md): Learn about the access rights you can grant to other users. See all access options for Apify resources such as Actors, tasks, storage, and schedules.
113: - [Organization account](https://docs.apify.com/account/collaboration/organization.md): Create a specialized account for your organization to encourage collaboration and manage permissions. Convert an existing account, or create one from scratch.
114: - [Using the organization account](https://docs.apify.com/account/collaboration/organization/how-to-use.md): Learn to use and manage your organization account using Apify Console or the Apify API. View the organizations you are in and manage your memberships.
115: - [Setup](https://docs.apify.com/account/collaboration/organization/setup.md): Configure your organization account by inviting new members and assigning their roles. Manage team members' access permissions to the organization's resources.
116: - [Apify Console](https://docs.apify.com/account/console.md): Get started with Apify Console: create an account, sign in with email, Google, or GitHub, and manage your web scraping projects from one place.
117: - [Limits](https://docs.apify.com/account/limits.md): View default resource limits for the Apify platform, including max memory, disk size, and number of Actors and tasks per user per plan tier.
118: - [Account settings](https://docs.apify.com/account/settings.md): Learn how to manage your Apify account, configure integrations, create and manage organizations, and set notification preferences in the Settings tab.
119: - [Apify subscription changes](https://docs.apify.com/account/subscription-changes.md): Learn what happens to the price and prepaid usage when you upgrade or downgrade your subscription plan or switch from monthly to annual billing.

127: - [Let your AI agent pay for Actor runs](https://docs.apify.com/agents/payments.md): Let an AI agent pay for Apify Actor runs without signing up, by buying a prepaid, spend-capped API token from Apify AGI with x402, MPP, a card, or Skyfire.

129: - [Agent quickstart](https://docs.apify.com/agents/quickstart.md): Connect your AI agent to the Apify MCP server, run your first Actor from a single prompt, and cap what a run your agent starts can cost you.
130: - [Resources for AI agents](https://docs.apify.com/agents/resources.md): Read Apify documentation programmatically through Markdown endpoints, llms.txt indexes, and MCP tools, and find every agent-facing file Apify publishes.
131: - [Apify Agent Skills](https://docs.apify.com/agents/skills.md): Install Apify Agent Skills to give a coding agent tested workflows for scraping, Actor development, actorization, and building Apify integrations.
132: ## console
133: - [Apify Store](https://docs.apify.com/console/store.md): Browse thousands of pre-built Actors in Apify Store, filter by category or pricing, and run them immediately or save settings for later use.

138: - [Run Actors](https://docs.apify.com/get-started/run-actors.md): Run existing Actors from Apify Store to get data or automate tasks with no code - pick an Actor, configure input, collect results, then automate.

140: - [Glossary](https://docs.apify.com/glossary.md): Definitions of Apify-specific terms, from Actors and datasets to proxy types and pricing models, each linking to the page that covers it in full.

144: - [Apify MCP server](https://docs.apify.com/mcp.md): Learn how to use the Apify MCP server to integrate Apify's library of Actors into your AI agents or large language model-based applications.

146: - [Proxy](https://docs.apify.com/proxy.md): Learn to anonymously access websites in scraping/automation jobs. Improve data outputs and efficiency of bots, and access websites from various geographies.
147: - [Datacenter proxy](https://docs.apify.com/proxy/datacenter-proxy.md): Learn how to reduce blocking when web scraping using IP address rotation. See proxy parameters and learn to implement Apify Proxy in an application.
148: - [Estimate how many datacenter IP addresses you need](https://docs.apify.com/proxy/estimate-ip-addresses.md): Estimate how many datacenter proxy IP addresses a job needs, compare the result with your plan, and get more with an add-on or a plan upgrade.
149: - [Google SERP proxy](https://docs.apify.com/proxy/google-serp-proxy.md): Learn how to collect search results from Google Search-powered tools. Get search results from localized domains in multiple countries, e.g. the US and Germany.
150: - [Residential proxy](https://docs.apify.com/proxy/residential-proxy.md): Achieve a higher level of anonymity using IP addresses from human users. Access a wider pool of proxies and reduce blocking by websites' anti-scraping measures.
151: - [Unblocker](https://docs.apify.com/proxy/unblocker.md): Bypass anti-bot and anti-captcha systems automatically when scraping, without building or maintaining your own bypass logic for blocked websites.
152: - [Use your own proxies](https://docs.apify.com/proxy/using-your-own-proxies.md): Add your own proxy URLs to Actor runs in Apify Console or configure them in the Apify SDK using the proxy configuration API for JavaScript and Python.

156: - [Shared responsibility model](https://docs.apify.com/security/shared-responsibility.md): How security responsibilities are divided between Apify and customers across the platform, your account, your Actors, and the data you collect.
157: - [Vulnerability disclosure policy](https://docs.apify.com/security/vulnerability-disclosure.md): Apify's vulnerability disclosure policy for the platform and open-source projects, including scope, testing guidelines, safe harbor, and how to report one.
158: ## storage
159: - [Storage](https://docs.apify.com/storage.md): Store anything from images and key-value pairs to structured output data. Learn how to access and manage your stored data from the Apify platform or via API.
160: - [Dataset](https://docs.apify.com/storage/dataset.md): Store and export web scraping, crawling or data processing job results. Learn how to access and manage datasets in Apify Console or via API.
161: - [Dataset schema specification](https://docs.apify.com/storage/dataset-schema.md): Define a dataset schema to control how your Actor's results are structured, validated, and displayed in Apify Console, the API, and integrations.
162: - [Use multiple datasets](https://docs.apify.com/storage/dataset-schema/multiple-datasets.md): Define more than one dataset in your Actor, write to each from your code, and surface them on the run page so users can find the right output.
163: - [Validate dataset output](https://docs.apify.com/storage/dataset-schema/validation.md): Specify the dataset schema within your Actors to add monitoring and validation at the field level, ensuring data quality and consistency across runs.
164: - [Key-value store](https://docs.apify.com/storage/key-value-store.md): Store anything from Actor or task run results, JSON documents, or images. Learn how to access and manage key-value stores from Apify Console or via API.
165: - [Key-value store schema specification](https://docs.apify.com/storage/key-value-store-schema.md): Define a key-value store schema to organize records into collections with content type validation, making your Actor's key-value store easier to navigate.
166: - [Request queue](https://docs.apify.com/storage/request-queue.md): Queue URLs for an Actor to visit in its run. Add requests in batches, lock them across runs, and manage request queues from Apify Console or via API.
167: - [Share storage](https://docs.apify.com/storage/share.md): Grant access rights to your storages, share them by link using their ID or name, and generate time-limited pre-signed URLs for restricted resources.

53: Apify command-line interface (Apify CLI) helps you create, develop, build and run Apify Actors, and manage the Apify platform from any computer.
54: What are Apify Actors?
55: Actors are cloud programs that can perform arbitrary web scraping, automation or data processing job. They accept input, perform their job and generate output.
56: Why use Apify CLI?
57: The Apify CLI enables you to develop Actors locally on your computer using your preferred tools:
58: Your favorite code editor
59: Version control system
60: Development tools and workflows
61: This gives you full control over your development environment and makes it easier to work on complex projects. You can leverage the Apify SDK with all its powerful features, then push your Actor to the Apify platform for deployment when ready.
62: Actor development environment
63: Actors run in Docker containers on the Apify platform. With an appropriate Dockerfile, you can build Actors in any programming language. We recommend JavaScript/Node.js and Python, for which we have the most comprehensive libraries and support.
64: Learn more
65: Learn everything you need to use the Apify CLI effectively:
66: Learn how to install the CLI on your system
67: Get started with your first Actor project

31: Copy for LLM
32: Actors are serverless cloud programs that take a structured JSON input, perform a task (web scraping, browser automation, data processing, and more), and optionally produce a structured output. Run them manually in Apify Console, through the API or CLI, or on a schedule, and combine them into larger automations.
33: Additional context
34: For more context, read the Actor whitepaper.
35: Actor lifecycle
36: Run Actors
37: Learn about Actor configuration, versioning, data retention, usage, and pricing.
38: Develop Actors
39: Learn about the technical part of building Apify Actors. Define Actor inputs, build new versions, persist Actor state, and choose base Docker images.
40: Publish Actors
41: Learn how to publish your Actor on Apify Store so that anyone can find and use it.
42: Monetize Actors
43: Learn how to choose a pricing model, set your Actor's price, and receive monthly payouts.
44: Promote Actors
45: Learn how to help users find and trust your Actor, from SEO to building credibility and reaching new audiences.
46: Actor components
47: Actors consist of these elements:
48: Dockerfile which specifies where the Actor's source code is, how to build it, and run it.
49: Documentation in a form of a README.md file.
50: Input and output schemas that describe what input the Actor requires, and what results it produces.
51: Access to an out-of-the-box storage system for Actor data, results, and files.
52: Metadata such as the Actor name, description, author, and version.
53: The documentation and input/output schemas help people understand what the Actor does, enter required inputs in the user interface or API, and integrate results into other workflows. Actors can call and interact with each other to build more complex systems from simple ones.
54: Public and private Actors
55: Actors can be public or private. Private Actors are yours to use and keep; no one will see them if you don't want them to. Public Actors are available to everyone in Apify Store. You can make them free to use, or you can charge for them.
56: Next steps

34: Integrations let you combine Apify Actors with the rest of your stack - workflow automation platforms, data warehouses, AI agents, and the tools your team already uses. The sections below mirror the integrations sidebar; each links through to the full list.
35: Actors
36: Connect Apify Actors to other Actors and tasks to build multi-step workflows directly on the platform. Set up integration-ready Actors that take run output from an upstream Actor and push it into a downstream system.
37: Actor-to-Actor
38: Trigger other Actors or tasks from your Actor's runs.
39: Integration-ready Actors
40: Build Actors that act as integration targets.
41: See all Actor integrations →
42: Programming
43: Drive the Apify platform programmatically with the REST API, react to platform events through webhooks, and trigger Actors from your GitHub activity.
44: API
45: Control the Apify platform programmatically from your code.
46: Webhooks
47: Trigger external events when an Actor run succeeds or fails.
48: GitHub
49: Trigger Apify runs from GitHub events.
50: See all Programming integrations →
51: AI
52: Connect any MCP client to Apify through the Apify MCP server, use Actors in agents built on SDKs and frameworks such as OpenAI Agents, LangChain, and the Vercel AI SDK, and load the results into vector databases for retrieval.
53: Apify MCP server
54: Expose Apify Actors and storages to any MCP-compatible AI client.
55: OpenAI Agents SDK
56: Use Apify Actors as tools in agents built on the OpenAI Agents SDK.

58: Wrap Apify Actors as LangChain tools for retrieval and agents.

60: Call Apify Actors from agents built on the Vercel AI SDK.

62: Add Apify Actors as tools in Google Agent Development Kit agents.

64: Embed and index scraped content in Pinecone for RAG.
65: See all AI integrations →

67: Set up Apify in an AI agent such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, with the Apify plugin or the MCP server and Agent Skills. To compare these options first, start at For AI agents.

69: Anthropic's chat assistant and its Claude Code coding agent.
70: ChatGPT/Codex
71: OpenAI's chat assistant and its Codex coding agent.
72: Cursor
73: AI code editor with a built-in coding agent.

75: Google's agentic development platform in the desktop app and CLI.

77: GitHub's AI coding agent in the CLI and desktop app.

79: Microsoft's code editor, with Copilot in agent mode.
80: OpenCode
81: Open-source coding agent that runs in your terminal.
82: Kimi Code
83: Moonshot AI's coding agent for the command line.
84: Qoder/Qwen
85: Alibaba's agentic coding platform and terminal agent.

87: DeepSeek's open-source agent harness for the terminal and web.

89: xAI's agentic coding tool that runs in your terminal.

93: Open-source personal AI assistant you run yourself.
94: Hermes Agent
95: Nous Research's open-source, self-improving agent.
96: See all agent integrations →

98: Send Apify Actor output to data warehouses, structured stores, CRMs, and shared drives where your team analyzes, models, and acts on it.
99: Snowflake
100: Stream Apify datasets straight into a Snowflake warehouse.
101: Airtable
102: Land Actor output as structured rows in Airtable bases.

104: Upload Actor datasets and exports to a shared Drive folder - a native Apify integration.
105: HubSpot
106: Enrich your HubSpot CRM with business contacts scraped from company websites.
107: See all Data and storage integrations →

109: Trigger Apify Actors from workflow automation platforms (n8n, Make, and Zapier), embed them as nodes in no-code agent builders, and route results into chat, email, and other team tools.
110: n8n
111: Run Apify Actors and route their data through n8n's node graph.
112: Make
113: Visual scenarios that connect Apify Actors with 1,500+ apps.
114: Zapier
115: Trigger Apify Actors from any of Zapier's 6,000+ apps.

117: Drag-and-drop agent builder with Apify Actors as nodes.

120: If you're building a service or platform and want your users to be able to connect it with Apify, create a new integration. The page walks through both routes - building an integration-ready Actor that other Apify users can plug into their workflows, or connecting your service to Apify externally via the API. If your team uses an AI coding agent, that page also covers the apify-integration-development skill, which guides the agent through the build.

42: Actor usage and resources
43: Copy for LLM
44: Resources
45: Actors run in Docker containers, which have a limited amount of resources (memory, CPU, disk size, etc). When starting, the Actor needs to be allocated a certain share of those resources, such as CPU capacity that is necessary for the Actor to run.
46: Assigning an Actor a specific Memory capacity, also determines the allocated CPU power and its disk size.
47: Check out the Limits page for detailed information on Actor memory, CPU limits, disk size and other limits.
48: Memory
49: When invoking an Actor, the caller can specify the memory allocation for the Actor run. If not specified, the Actor's default memory is used (which can be dynamic). The memory allocation must follow these requirements:
50: It must be a power of 2.
51: The minimum allowed value is 128MB
52: The maximum allowed value is 32768MB
53: Acceptable values include: 128MB, 256MB, 512MB, 1024MB, 2048MB, 4096MB, 8192MB, 16384MB, and 32768MB
54: Additionally, each user has a certain total limit of memory for running Actors. The sum of memory allocated for all running Actors and builds needs to be within this limit, otherwise the user cannot start a new Actor. For more details, see limits.
55: CPU
56: The CPU allocation for an Actor is automatically computed based on the assigned memory, following these rules:
57: For every 4096MB of memory, the Actor receives one full CPU core
58: If the memory allocation is not a multiple of 4096MB, the CPU core allocation is calculated proportionally
59: Examples:
60: 512MB = 1/8 of a CPU core
61: 1024MB = 1/4 of a CPU core
62: 8192MB = 2 CPU cores
63: CPU usage spikes
64: Sometimes, you see the Actor's CPU use go over 100%. This is not unusual. To help an Actor start up faster, it is allocated a free CPU boost. For example, if an Actor is assigned 1GB (25% of a core), it will temporarily be allowed to use 100% of the core, so it gets started quicker.
65: Disk
66: The Actor has hard disk space limited by twice the amount of memory. For example, an Actor with 1024MB of memory will have 2048MB of disk available.
67: Choose memory for your Actor
68: Actors built with Crawlee use autoscaling, which adjusts how many requests Actors process in parallel to the memory and CPU they get. If you double the memory, the run finishes in about half the time and uses the same number of compute units: 1 GB × 1 hour = 2 GB × 0.5 hours = 1 CU.
69: Start with 4096 MB. To get results faster, increase the memory. To reduce the load on the target website, decrease the memory.
70: Autoscaling only helps runs that process many URLs for at least 30 seconds. For Actors that scrape one URL or do a single isolated job, use less memory.
71: To estimate how many compute units your project needs, see Estimate resource consumption.
72: Minimum memory
73: Each use case has its own memory requirements. The larger and more complex your project, the more memory/CPU power it will require. Some examples which have minimum requirements are:
74: Actors using Puppeteer or Playwright for real web browser rendering require at least 1024MB of memory.
75: Large and complex sites like Google Maps require at least 4096MB for optimal speed and concurrency.
76: Projects involving large amount of data in memory.
77: Maximum memory
78: Apify Actors are most commonly written in Node.js, which uses a single thread process. Unless you use external binaries such as the Chrome browser, Puppeteer, Playwright, or other multi-threaded libraries you will not gain more CPU power from assigning your Actor more than 4096MB of memory because Node.js cannot use more than 1 core.
79: In other words, giving a Cheerio-based crawler 16384MB of memory (4 CPU cores) will not improve its performance, because these crawlers cannot use more than 1 CPU core.
80: Multi-threaded Node.js configuration
81: It's possible to use multiple threads in Node.js-based Actor with some configuration. This can be useful if you need to offload a part of your workload.
82: Usage
83: When you run an Actor it generates platform usage that's charged to the user account. Platform usage comprises four main parts:
84: Compute units: Memory allocated to the Actor run or build, multiplied by how long the run lasts.
85: Data transfer: The amount of data transferred between the web, Apify platform, and other external systems.
86: Proxy costs: Residential or SERP proxy usage.
87: Storage operations: Read, write, and other operations performed on the Key-value store, Dataset, and Request queue.
88: The platform usage can be represented either in raw units (e.g. gigabytes for data transfer, or number of writes for dataset operations), or in the dollar equivalents.
89: To view the usage of an Actor run, navigate to the Runs section and check out the Usage column.
90: For a more detailed breakdown, click on the specific run you want to examine and then on the ? icon next to the Usage label.
91: Usage billing elements
92: For technical reasons, when viewing the usage in dollars for a specific historical Actor run or build in the API or Apify Console, your current service pricing is used to compute the dollar amount.
93: This should be used for informational purposes only.
94: For detailed information, FAQ, and, pricing check out the platform pricing page.

39: You can securely share your resources with others by using a granular permissions system. Such resources include Actors, tasks, key-value stores, datasets, and request queues.
40: For example, you can let your colleague run an Actor or view a dataset but not modify it. You can also grant permission to update an Actor and build a new version. Storages are sharable in the same way as a read permission or a combination of both read and write permissions.
41: Grant access to resources
42: To share an Actor or a task:
43: In Apify Console, go to the Actor or task page.
44: From the menu, select Share.
45: Under Invite, add the user ID, email, or username of a person you want to share the resource with and select Add user.
46: From the dropdown, select the permissions to grant.
47: To share a key-value store, request queue, or a dataset:
48: In Apify Console, in the left-side menu, go to Storage.
49: Use tabs to switch between datasets, key-value stores, and request queues.
50: From the table, select the resource you want to share.
51: Under Invite, add the user ID, email, or username of a person you want to share the resource with and select Add user.
52: From the dropdown, select the permissions to grant.
53: Transfer an Actor between accounts
54: To transfer your Actor to another Apify account, contact support. The transfer keeps the Actor's reviews and usage statistics.
55: Note that the Actor's URL in Apify Store changes, as it includes the account ID. The Actor's URL in Apify Console stays the same.

36: The Apify API client is the official library to access the Apify REST API from your JavaScript/TypeScript applications. It runs both in Node.js and browser and provides useful features like automatic retries and convenience functions that improve the experience of using the Apify API.
37: The client simplifies interaction with the Apify platform by providing:
38: Intuitive methods for working with Actors, datasets, key-value stores, and other Apify resources
39: Intelligent parsing of API responses and rich error messages for debugging
40: Built-in exponential backoff for failed requests
41: Full TypeScript support with comprehensive type definitions
42: Cross-platform compatibility in Node.js v16+ and modern browsers
43: All requests and responses (including errors) are encoded in JSON format with UTF-8 encoding.
44: Pre-requisites
45: apify-client requires Node.js version 16 or higher. Node.js is available for download on the official website. Check for your current Node.js version by running:
46: node -v
47: Installation
48: You can install the client via NPM or any other package manager of your choice.
49: NPM
50: Yarn
51: PNPM
52: Bun
53: npm i apify-client
54: yarn add apify-client
55: pnpm add apify-client
56: bun add apify-client
57: Quick example
58: Here's an example showing how to run an Actor and retrieve its results:
59: import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';
60: // Initialize the client with your API token
61: const client = new ApifyClient({
62: token: 'MY-APIFY-TOKEN',
63: });
64: // Start an Actor and wait for it to finish
65: const run = await client.actor('apify/web-scraper').call({
66: startUrls: [{ url: 'https://example.com' }],
67: maxCrawlPages: 10,
68: });
69: // Get results from the Actor's dataset
70: const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
71: console.log(items);
72: You can find your API token in the Integrations section of Apify Console. See the Quick start guide for more details on authentication.

40: The Apify API client for Python is the official library to access the Apify REST API from your Python applications. It provides useful features like automatic retries and convenience functions that improve the experience of using the Apify API.
41: The client simplifies interaction with the Apify platform by providing:
42: Intuitive methods for working with Actors, Datasets, Key-value stores, and other Apify resources
43: Both synchronous and asynchronous interfaces for flexible integration
44: Built-in retries with exponential backoff for failed requests
45: Comprehensive API coverage with JSON encoding (UTF-8) for all requests and responses
46: Prerequisites
47: apify-client requires Python 3.11 or higher. Python is available for download on the official website. Check your current Python version by running:
48: python --version
49: Installation
50: The Apify client is available as the apify-client package on PyPI or on conda-forge.
51: PyPI
52: conda-forge
53: pip install apify-client
54: conda install conda-forge::apify-client
55: For better request-body compression, opt in to brotli, which compresses better than gzip, especially for large payloads. Install the optional extra:
56: PyPI
57: conda-forge
58: pip install "apify-client[brotli]"
59: conda install conda-forge::apify-client
60: For details, see HTTP compression.
61: The client uses Impit as its default HTTP transport. To use the built-in HTTPX2 transport, install the optional httpx2 extra, which provides Pydantic's maintained continuation of HTTPX:
62: PyPI
63: conda-forge
64: pip install "apify-client[httpx2]"
65: conda install conda-forge::apify-client conda-forge::httpx2
66: For synchronous and asynchronous examples and details about the shared architecture, see HTTP clients.
67: Quick example
68: The following example shows how to run an Actor and retrieve its results:
69: Async client
70: Sync client
71: from apify_client import ApifyClientAsync
72: # You can find your API token at https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations.
73: TOKEN = 'MY-APIFY-TOKEN'
74: async def main() -> None:
75: apify_client = ApifyClientAsync(TOKEN)
76: # Start an Actor and wait for it to finish.
77: actor_client = apify_client.actor('john-doe/my-cool-actor')
78: call_result = await actor_client.call()
79: if call_result is None:
80: print('Actor run failed.')
81: return
82: # Fetch results from the Actor run's default dataset.
83: dataset_client = apify_client.dataset(call_result.default_dataset_id)
84: list_items_result = await dataset_client.list_items()
85: print(f'Dataset: {list_items_result}')
86: from apify_client import ApifyClient

88: TOKEN = 'MY-APIFY-TOKEN'

375: Frequently asked questions
376: Got questions? We're glad to hear that because we have answers.
377: What is the prepaid platform usage, and how much do I need?
378: The Apify platform has a number of services that are charged based on usages, such as Actors, proxies, data transfer, and storage. See pricing for the full list of platform services.
379: Each subscription plan comes with a certain amount of prepaid platform usage that is used to pay for services. If your platform usage in a given billing cycle exceeds this prepaid amount, the excess usage will be added to your next invoice, and you'll get a notification. If you're on the free plan, your access to Apify's services will be blocked until the beginning of the next monthly cycle.
380: Note that unused usage credits are not rolled over to the next billing cycle, and they expire at the end of the billing cycle.
381: Can I try Apify for free?
382: Absolutely! We offer a free plan that lets you use most of the features of the Apify platform, but with certain limits. No credit card is required. The free plan includes Apify Proxy, which is limited to use within the platform and does not extend to external clients.
383: If you'd like a free demo of Apify's custom solutions, please contact us.
384: Which plan should I choose?
385: If you're unsure which plan is right for you, just pick the lowest-priced plan that has all the features you need. If you exceed the prepaid platform usage, you'll get a notification, and the excess usage will be added to the next invoice (see below for details).
386: You can upgrade to a higher plan at any time in your Billing settings, and you'll only pay for the price difference.
387: What is the pricing for Actors in Apify Store?
388: Every Actor in Apify Store uses one of two pricing models, and each Actor's page states which one applies to it.
389: Pay per event - you pay a fixed price for the events the Actor's developer defines, such as starting the Actor or returning a single result. Most pay-per-event Actors include the Apify platform usage in the event price, but some charge for it separately, so check the pricing section on the Actor's page.
390: Pay per usage - the developer charges nothing on top, and you only pay for the platform usage consumed by the Actor's runs: compute units, data transfer, storage operations, and residential or SERP proxies.
391: Both models draw on the platform usage credits included in your plan, and excess usage is charged to your next invoice. Reading from or writing to a run's dataset after the run finishes also counts as platform usage.
392: The exact platform usage depends on the specific Actor, the type of job it performs, how often it runs, and for how long. The easiest way to find out the platform usage of an Actor is to perform a test run. You can then review your platform usage in your Billing settings and figure out the best subscription plan for your needs.
393: For a full breakdown of both models, see Actors in Apify Store. If you need advice, please contact us.
394: Can an AI agent pay for Actor runs without an Apify account?
395: Yes. An autonomous agent with a crypto wallet can pay through the agentic payment protocols x402 and MPP, with no account and no human sign-up. The agent pays once at agi.apify.com, receives a temporary Apify API token with a fixed spend cap, and calls the Apify API with it like any other token. Each Actor run is metered against that prepaid balance, and unused balance expires with the token.
396: Agents find the complete, current instructions, including supported chains, terms, and balance checks, at agi.apify.com/AGENTS.md.
397: Can I upgrade, downgrade or cancel my plan?
398: You can upgrade, downgrade, or cancel your plan at any time in your Billing settings.
399: When you upgrade, your payment will be prorated, so you will only pay for the difference between the old and the new price, taking into account how much of the billing cycle has already passed.
400: When you downgrade, there's no proration except for the unused platform usage that's rolled over to the new plan.
401: If you decide to cancel, your subscription will last until the end of the current billing cycle. It won't be renewed after that. Note that you might still be charged for excess platform usage.
402: What drives the cost of an Actor run?
403: Most Actors in Apify Store use pay-per-event pricing. You pay the prices listed on the Actor's page for events such as returning a result. Pay-per-usage Actors and your own Actors bill platform usage instead, including compute units, storage, proxies, and data transfer. Some pay-per-event Actors charge both. You can check your daily usage chart on the Apify platform.
404: What happens after I run out of prepaid usage?
405: If you're a paying user, you can continue using the platform and will be charged for overage until you reach the usage limit configured in the billing. If you're on the free plan, you'll be blocked until the next billing cycle.
406: What happens to my prepaid usage if I don't use all of it?
407: If you don't consume all your prepaid usage, it disappears at the end of the billing cycle. Go to our pricing page to learn more about the prepaid usage of all Apify's subscription plans.
408: Why do some of my Actor runs cost more than others?
409: On a pay-per-event Actor, a run costs more when it returns more results or triggers more events. When you pay for platform usage, the cost depends on proxies, data transfers, memory, and run duration. It also depends on the number of retries when a request fails.
410: How does Apify pay as you go work?
411: If you're on one of Apify's paid plans, you can continue using the platform after reaching the limit by paying the rest as overage. That means you don't have to change your pricing plan to exceed the usage limit of your current plan.
412: Does Apify offer any discounts for universities or nonprofit organizations?
413: Apify offers discounts on its paid plans to both academic institutions and nonprofit organizations. Students are eligible for 50% off Starter, Scale, and Business plans, while nonprofits can get a personalized discount. Learn more at Apify for universities and Apify for nonprofits.
414: Do startups get the same pricing as enterprise customers?
415: Apify believes in encouraging startups to grow by using online data at scale. So we're giving a special 30% discount on our Scale plan to startups. Learn more at Apify for startups.
416: I would like to develop Actors. What should I do?
417: Apify Academy is a free course that shows you how to start developing Actors on the Apify platform. You can also find more information in the Apify documentation.
418: Couldn't find something? Message us.

220: Apify MCP server
221: Connect your agent to the largest marketplace of tools for AI.
222: The official Apify Model Context Protocol (MCP) server gives AI agents web scraping, data extraction, and browser automation through thousands of ready-made Actors from Apify Store, at https://mcp.apify.com.
223: Apify is the marketplace of ready-to-run tools for AI agents. One connection to the Apify MCP server gives your agent thousands of tools to choose from, for jobs like web fetch, SERP monitoring, lead generation and enrichment, and pulling data from e-commerce sites and social media. The server loads only what each task needs.
224: Your agent searches Apify Store, checks an Actor's input and pricing, runs it, and reads the structured results, so you don't install a separate MCP server for every site. Connect to the hosted server with OAuth, or run it locally over stdio with the @apify/actors-mcp-server npm package.

242: 🚀 Quickstart
243: Open the MCP configurator, pick your client, and choose the tools you want.
244: Copy the generated configuration, deeplink, or command into your client.
245: Sign in to Apify in the browser window that opens. If you don't have an account, you can create a free one there.
246: The hosted endpoint is https://mcp.apify.com. If your client can't use OAuth, send your Apify API token in an Authorization: Bearer <APIFY_TOKEN> header instead. Treat the token like a password and keep it out of repositories. Create a token in Apify Console and copy it right after creating it. It is shown only once.
247: Using a coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or GitHub Copilot? An official Apify plugin installs this MCP server together with Apify agent skills in one step.
248: 🤖 Set up your client
249: The configurator generates the exact setup for each supported client, including Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude, Claude Desktop, Codex, OpenCode, Kiro, and more. The snippets below cover the most common cases.
250: Claude Code
251: claude mcp add apify "https://mcp.apify.com" -t http
252: Claude Code opens the Apify sign-in page the first time it uses the server. To install the Apify plugin with Apify agent skills instead, run /plugin marketplace add apify/apify-claude-code-plugin, then /plugin install apify@apify and /reload-plugins.
253: ChatGPT
254: Open ChatGPT Plugins, select Add in the top-right corner, then Add custom MCP server.
255: Fill in the form:
256: Icon: upload the Apify icon.
257: Name: Apify
258: Description: Extract data from any website with thousands of scrapers, crawlers, and automations on Apify Store
259: Connection: Server URL, the URL with your settings from the configurator, for example with ?tools=. Without custom settings, use https://mcp.apify.com.
260: Authentication: OAuth
261: Check I understand and want to continue, then select Create as a plugin.
262: Sign in with Apify, review the tools, and install the plugin. No API token is needed.
263: Start a new conversation, type @, and select Apify.
264: In Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces, an admin or owner may need to create or publish the plugin. If the option is missing, ask your workspace admin. When the server's tools change, open the plugin and select Refresh.
265: The ChatGPT desktop app uses local MCP configuration shared with Codex instead: go to Settings > MCP servers > Add server, choose Streamable HTTP, and enter https://mcp.apify.com. See OpenAI's custom MCP server guide.
266: Cursor
267: Add Apify to Cursor, or let the Apify CLI write the configuration, including your API token:
268: apify mcp install cursor
269: The same command works for claude-code, vscode, codex, kiro, and antigravity.
270: VS Code and GitHub Copilot
271: Use the one-click install link from the configurator, run apify mcp install vscode, or add https://mcp.apify.com as an HTTP server in your MCP configuration:

273: "servers": {

275: "type": "http",
276: "url": "https://mcp.apify.com"
277: }

280: Claude
281: Add Apify to Claude: the link opens the custom connector dialog with the name and URL filled in. Sign in with Apify when prompted.
282: To set it up by hand, open Settings > Connectors, select Add custom connector, name it Apify, and enter https://mcp.apify.com as the remote MCP server URL. The same connector works on Claude.ai and in Claude Desktop. See the Claude guide.

306: If you've run apify login, the server can also read the token saved by the Apify CLI. Run npx @apify/actors-mcp-server --help for all options.
307: The server is also listed in the Docker MCP catalog, and each release ships an MCP bundle file (apify-mcp-server.mcpb) for one-click installation in clients that support it.

Use the local server when you want to run the MCP process on your own machine; Actors still run and store their results on the Apify platform in both modes. If your client supports only stdio, you can also bridge it to the hosted server with mcp-remote: npx mcp-remote https://mcp.apify.com.

327: How an agent uses Apify Actors
328: Actors are serverless programs on the Apify platform. Each one does a specific job, like scraping Google Maps, crawling a website for RAG, or collecting social media posts. The MCP server turns Actors into tools an agent can find and call without you configuring each one in advance.
329: A typical task follows four steps:
330: search-actors finds candidate Actors in Apify Store for the task.
331: fetch-actor-details returns the Actor's input schema, README, and pricing, plus its output schema on request.
332: call-actor starts the run and waits for it to finish, 30 seconds by default and up to 45. It returns the run status and storage IDs; the scraped items stay in the run's dataset.
333: get-dataset-items reads the results from the run's dataset, with limit and offset for pagination.
334: The server adds get-dataset-items, get-key-value-store-record, get-actor-run, and abort-actor-run whenever call-actor or an Actor tool is loaded, so the agent can always read results and check on long runs that outlast the wait.
335: You can also expose a specific Actor as its own tool, for example apify/instagram-scraper. The server builds the tool's parameters from the Actor's input schema, so the agent knows exactly what to pass. A Server Actor with an API schema, such as apify/web-fetch, apify/web-search, or apify/rag-web-browser, gets a tool that sends one HTTP request to its API instead.
336: Actors that run their own MCP server. Some Actors are MCP servers themselves. fetch-actor-mcp-tool-list lists their tools, and call-actor-mcp-tool calls one. When such an Actor is loaded as a tool source and has no API schema, its tools are exposed under names in the form username--actor-name--tool-name; an Actor with an API schema, such as apify/web-search, gets its server tool instead, and call-actor-mcp-tool reaches its MCP tools. Apify Store also lists MCP-related Actors from independent creators; those are separate products with their own READMEs and pricing.
337: 🛠️ Tools, resources, and prompts
338: Any Actor can be a tool, and agents discover new ones as they work. By default, the server loads the actors and docs categories, two Actor tools (Web Search and Web Fetch), and report-problem. Everything else is opt-in by category or by tool name.
339: Helper tools
340: Besides Actor tools, the server provides helper tools for the Apify platform:
341: Actors: search Apify Store, list the Actors in your account, view their details, call tools on Actors that run MCP servers, send requests to Server Actors, and delete your own Actors.
342: Documentation: search the Apify and Crawlee docs and fetch pages as context.
343: Runs and storage: list runs, inspect them, read their logs, and read datasets and key-value stores.
344: Tasks and schedules: manage saved Actor tasks and their public landing pages, and schedules that run Actors and tasks automatically.
345: Builds and versions: build Actors, read build logs, and create, read, change, copy, and delete versions from files.
346: Apify API: search the API reference, inspect an operation, and send requests to read or change data.
