515: The tasks category manages saved Actor tasks. It is unrelated to the MCP Tasks protocol. The tool reference has full descriptions of each tool.
516: Tool annotations
517: Every tool carries a title, a readOnlyHint, and an openWorldHint. readOnlyHint is true for tools that only read data. Actor tools get it only for Apify-maintained Actors with limited permissions and no inputs that accept secrets, writable storage, an MCP connector, or code; other Actor tools are marked destructive. openWorldHint is true for tools that reach outside the Apify platform, such as call-actor, and false for platform-only tools.
518: Prompts and resources
519: No prompts are registered yet, so prompts/list returns an empty list. resources/read accepts any Apify API GET URL (https://api.apify.com/v2/...) and returns the response body using the session's Apify token, inlined up to 256 KB. Your data isn't enumerated in resources/list; resources/templates/list lists the common shapes with their paging parameters.
520: Choose which tools load
521: The tools parameter takes categories, tool names, and Actor names, separated by commas. When you set it, the defaults are dropped and only what you list is loaded, plus the ⚡ run and storage tools whenever the list includes call-actor or an Actor. The easiest way to build a selection is the configurator.
522: Hosted server:
523: https://mcp.apify.com?tools=actors,docs,apify/web-search,apify/web-fetch
524: Local server:
525: npx @apify/actors-mcp-server --tools actors,docs,apify/web-search,apify/web-fetch
526: To give an agent a single Actor, list only that Actor. The agent gets its tool plus the four ⚡ tools it needs to read the results:
527: https://mcp.apify.com?tools=apify/instagram-scraper
528: Pin your tools in production. The default tool set can change between versions. Set tools explicitly if you need a stable interface.
529: Backward compatibility with older configurations
530: apify/web-search replaced apify/rag-web-browser in the default tools. To keep apify--rag-web-browser, add apify/rag-web-browser to your tools list, or set tools=actors,docs,apify/rag-web-browser,apify/web-fetch for the previous default categories and Actors.
531: The actors URL parameter and --actors flag still work. They're merged into tools, so ?actors=apify/web-fetch equals ?tools=apify/web-fetch.
532: enableAddingActors, enable-adding-actors, and enableActorAutoLoading were removed and are ignored. Dynamic Actor calls come from call-actor, which the default actors category includes.
533: The selectors add-actor, experimental, and preview are retired and load nothing. Use call-actor or the actors category.
534: get-actor-log was renamed to get-actor-run-log, and the source category to versions. The old names load nothing.
535: call-actor no longer calls tools on MCP server Actors: the actorName:toolName form is rejected. Use call-actor-mcp-tool with actor, tool, and arguments. call-actor still starts a run of an MCP server Actor that has an input schema; one without is refused. A selection that names call-actor alone needs call-actor-mcp-tool added.
536: fetch-actor-details no longer lists an MCP server Actor's tools, and output.mcpTools is ignored. Use fetch-actor-mcp-tool-list, which returns the definitions in structuredContent.tools. A selection that names fetch-actor-details alone needs fetch-actor-mcp-tool-list added.
537: A selected Actor with an API schema (a Server Actor) gets a tool that sends one HTTP request to its API, with method, path, and query arguments, instead of a tool that starts a run. If the Actor is also an MCP server, the selection no longer loads its MCP tools: use call-actor-mcp-tool. call-actor still starts runs of the Actor when it has an input schema. A selected apify/rag-web-browser is served this way too, with GET /search.
538: apify--web-fetch sends one HTTP request to the Web Fetch Actor's API instead of starting a run, and returns the HTTP response. Its arguments are method, path, query and, for POST /, body, for example {"method": "GET", "path": "/", "query": {"url": "https://example.com", "formats": ["markdown", "links"]}}.
539: apify--web-search sends one HTTP request to the Web Search Actor's API instead of starting a run, and returns the HTTP response. Its arguments are method, path, query and, for POST /, body, for example {"method": "GET", "path": "/", "query": {"query": "AI agent payment protocols", "maxResults": 5}}. call-actor still starts runs of the Actor, and call-actor-mcp-tool calls its search MCP tool.
540: UI mode configuration
541: The ui parameter controls MCP Apps widget tools. With UI mode on, the server adds search-actors-widget and fetch-actor-details-widget next to their base tools, which keep returning standard responses. By default (auto), UI mode turns on when the client supports MCP Apps.
542: Value
543: Behavior
544: auto (default)
545: Widget tools added when the client supports MCP Apps
546: true, on, or apps
547: Widget tools always added
548: false, off, or default
549: No widget tools
550: Hosted server:
551: https://mcp.apify.com?tools=actors,docs&ui=true
552: Local server, with a CLI flag or the UI_MODE environment variable:
553: npx @apify/actors-mcp-server --ui true
554: UI_MODE=true npx @apify/actors-mcp-server
555: 💬 Example prompts
556: Ask in plain language. The agent finds a suitable Actor, checks its input and pricing, runs it, and reads the results. These prompts cover the most common jobs:
557: Use case
558: Example prompt
559: Example Actor
560: Web research
561: "Find what people on X said about autonomous AI agents this week and summarize the key developments."
562: Tweet Scraper V2
563: Search and read the web
564: "Compare the current pricing plans of Notion, Coda, and Airtable and tell me which is cheapest for a 10-person team."
565: Web Search, Web Fetch
566: Search results (SERP)
567: "Get the top 20 Google results for 'best CRM for startups' in the US and show who ranks where."
568: Google Search Results Scraper
569: Lead generation
570: "Find dentists in Austin, Texas on Google Maps with their phone numbers, websites, and ratings."
571: Google Maps Scraper
572: LinkedIn profiles
573: "Get the current job title, company, and work history for these 20 LinkedIn profiles."
574: LinkedIn Profile Scraper
575: LinkedIn company posts
576: "Get the 30 latest posts from Apify's LinkedIn company page with their reaction counts."
577: LinkedIn Company Posts Scraper
578: Review analysis
579: "Pull the latest 100 Google Maps reviews for this hotel and group the complaints by theme."
580: Google Maps Reviews Scraper
581: Social media monitoring
582: "Get the 50 latest posts from @nasa on Instagram with likes and comments."
583: Instagram Scraper
584: Trend research
585: "Find the most viewed TikTok videos for #skincare this week."
586: TikTok Scraper
587: E-commerce
588: "List the 10 best-rated wireless earbuds on Amazon with prices and review counts."
589: Amazon Product Scraper
590: Knowledge base and RAG
591: "Crawl docs.example.com and turn every page into Markdown I can load into my vector database."
592: Website Content Crawler
593: Follow-ups work too. "Show me the next 10 results from that run" makes the agent call get-dataset-items again with a higher offset. With the schedules category loaded, "Run that Google Maps search every Monday at 9 am" creates a schedule.
594: 💰 Pricing and limits
595: Connecting to the MCP server is free. Actor runs bill to your Apify account according to each Actor's pricing, which fetch-actor-details shows before a run. The Apify free plan includes $5 of monthly platform usage.
596: To cap what a run can cost, pass maxTotalChargeUsd (pay-per-event Actors) or maxItems (pay-per-result Actors) in the callOptions of call-actor. timeout and memory limit the run's duration and memory, not its price.
597: The hosted server accepts up to 20 requests per second per account.
598: search-actors returns only free and pay-per-event Actors that pass the platform's agent-safety filters, so rental and pay-per-result Actors don't appear in search. Full-permission Actors need your one-time approval; until then, call-actor returns an error with an approval link.
599: Some tools work without an Apify account: search-actors, fetch-actor-details, search-apify-docs, fetch-apify-docs, apify-api-search, and apify-api-details. Select only those, for example https://mcp.apify.com?tools=search-actors, and the hosted server accepts the connection without a token.
600: 🪙 Agentic payments (experimental). Agents can pay for Actor runs without an Apify account. AGI sells a prepaid, spend-capped Apify API token for an x402, MPP, or Skyfire payment. The agent then uses it as a normal Bearer token against mcp.apify.com, with any Actor that uses limited permissions. See the agentic payments documentation for supported methods and limits, and agi.apify.com/AGENTS.md for protocol details.
601: 📡 Telemetry
602: The Apify MCP server collects telemetry about tool calls to help Apify understand usage patterns and improve the service. Telemetry is on by default. With telemetry on, Actor searches in Apify Store send the first 12 hex characters of the SHA-256 hash of the MCP session ID as _traceId, and tool-call events carry it as trace_id. search-actors also sends _useCase, a one-sentence reason for the search written by the model, which Apify uses to improve Store search results. The stdio transport also uses Sentry for error tracking, which helps the Apify team find and fix issues faster.
603: To opt out, including Sentry, set the telemetry-enabled URL parameter or the --telemetry-enabled CLI flag to false, or set TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false. CLI flags take precedence over environment variables.
604: https://mcp.apify.com?telemetry-enabled=false
605: npx @apify/actors-mcp-server --telemetry-enabled=false
606: TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false npx @apify/actors-mcp-server
607: 🐛 Troubleshooting and limitations
608: The local server won't start. Check your Node.js version: the package requires Node.js 22 or later.
609: Authentication fails. Reconnect so the client repeats the OAuth flow, or switch to a Bearer token. For the local server, check that APIFY_TOKEN is set in the client's server configuration, not only in your shell.
610: VS Code says the OAuth app is not registered. Run Authentication: Remove Dynamic Authentication Providers, select Apify, and sign in again.
611: Client features vary. Any MCP client can connect, but support for dynamic tool lists, OAuth, and MCP Apps differs between clients.
612: Invalid Actor input. When call-actor fails because of invalid input, the error includes the Actor's input schema so the agent can correct the input and retry.
613: How the server adapts Actor input schemas
614: The server adapts Actor input schemas so that more clients and models can use them:
615: Descriptions longer than 500 characters are cut at the last complete sentence and marked [Description truncated].
616: Enums are kept in full up to 2,000 combined characters. Larger enums are replaced by a short note with example values.
617: Required fields get a REQUIRED prefix in their descriptions for frameworks that ignore the JSON Schema required list.
618: Nested properties are built for special inputs such as proxy configuration and request lists.
619: Missing array item types are inferred from the item type, the prefill, the default value, or the editor type, in that order.
620: Prefill and default values are copied into descriptions as examples, for clients that ignore JSON Schema examples.
621: For more help, see the MCP documentation or open an issue.
622: ❓ FAQ
623: What is an MCP server?
624: An MCP server exposes tools and data to AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, an open standard supported by clients such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor. The agent connects once and calls the server's tools when a task needs them. The Apify MCP server's tools are the Actors in Apify Store.
625: What is the Apify MCP server?
626: It's the official Model Context Protocol server for Apify. It lets AI agents search Apify Store, run Actors for web scraping, data extraction, and browser automation, and read the structured results.
627: When is it a good MCP server for web scraping?
628: When an agent needs data from many different sites. A typical case is Google Maps one day, Instagram or an online store the next. The agent picks a ready-made Actor for each site from Apify Store instead of you writing and maintaining a scraper. Each Actor works like a web scraping API for its site, and the Apify platform handles scaling, proxies, and storage of the results.
629: How does it compare to Playwright MCP?
630: Playwright MCP drives a browser on your machine step by step, through clicks and page snapshots. The Apify MCP server runs Actors in the Apify cloud. Each Actor handles JavaScript rendering, proxies, and blocking for its site and returns structured results, so the agent asks for the data instead of operating a browser. Many agents use both.
631: Can ChatGPT or Claude scrape websites with it?
632: Yes. Connect ChatGPT, Claude, or Claude Code to https://mcp.apify.com, then ask in plain language. The model searches for a suitable Actor, runs it, and reads the results.
633: Is it free?
634: Connecting is free, and some discovery tools work without an account. Actor runs bill to your Apify account at each Actor's price, and the free plan includes $5 of monthly platform usage.
635: Do I need an API token?
636: Not with the hosted server, because OAuth signs you in through the browser. The local server needs APIFY_TOKEN or an Apify CLI login.
637: Can I limit what the agent can do or spend?
638: Yes. Select tools with the tools parameter or expose a single Actor. To cap a run's cost, pass maxTotalChargeUsd for pay-per-event Actors or maxItems for pay-per-result Actors in call-actor options.
639: 🔧 Development
640: This repository contains the open-source server package published to npm as @apify/actors-mcp-server. The hosted service at mcp.apify.com runs on this core logic from a separate private repository.
641: You need Node.js 22 or later and pnpm.
642: pnpm install
643: pnpm run build
644: pnpm run dev # Streamable HTTP server on http://localhost:3001, hot reload for widgets
645: pnpm run inspector:stdio # MCP Inspector against the stdio server
646: The development HTTP server doesn't read APIFY_TOKEN from the environment. Pass your token in an Authorization: Bearer header or a ?token= query parameter, for example from the MCP Inspector.
647: To publish a canary build of a pull request to pkg.pr.new, add the beta label to it.
648: DEVELOPMENT.md covers the project structure, tool loading phases, the Node.js version policy, and testing.
649: 🤝 Contributing
650: Bug reports, feature requests, and documentation fixes are welcome. Open an issue with steps to reproduce a bug, or describe the problem a feature would solve and who runs into it. Send typos, broken links, and wrong commands straight to a pull request. For code, work only on an issue a maintainer has invited you to pick up; unsolicited pull requests are closed.
651: Read CONTRIBUTING.md before you start, including the rules for AI-assisted contributions.
652: 🔒 Privacy and license
653: Requests and Actor inputs go to the Apify API to run the Actors you call. Apify doesn't share them with third parties beyond what running those Actors requires. See Apify legal documents for details on data collection and retention.
654: The project is licensed under the MIT license.

19: # Apify MCP server 20: Connect your agent to the largest marketplace of tools for AI. 21: **The official Apify Model Context Protocol (MCP) server gives AI agents web scraping, data extraction, and browser automation through thousands of ready-made Actors from [Apify Store](https://apify.com/store), at [`https://mcp.apify.com`](https://mcp.apify.com).** 22: Apify is the marketplace of ready-to-run tools for AI agents. One connection to the Apify MCP server gives your agent thousands of tools to choose from, for jobs like web fetch, SERP monitoring, lead generation and enrichment, and pulling data from e-commerce sites and social media. The server loads only what each task needs. 23: Your agent searches Apify Store, checks an Actor's input and pricing, runs it, and reads the structured results, so you don't install a separate MCP server for every site. Connect to the hosted server with OAuth, or run it locally over stdio with the [`@apify/actors-mcp-server`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@apify/actors-mcp-server) npm package. 24: 25: 26: ## Contents 27: - [Quickstart](#-quickstart) 28: - [Set up your client](#-set-up-your-client) 29: - [Remote (hosted) or local MCP server](#remote-hosted-or-local-mcp-server) 30: - [How an agent uses Apify Actors](#how-an-agent-uses-apify-actors) 31: - [Tools, resources, and prompts](#%EF%B8%8F-tools-resources-and-prompts) 32: - [Choose which tools load](#choose-which-tools-load) 33: - [UI mode configuration](#ui-mode-configuration) 34: - [Example prompts](#-example-prompts) 35: - [Pricing and limits](#-pricing-and-limits) 36: - [Telemetry](#-telemetry) 37: - [Troubleshooting and limitations](#-troubleshooting-and-limitations) 38: - [FAQ](#-faq) 39: - [Development](#-development) 40: - [Contributing](#-contributing) 41: - [Privacy and license](#-privacy-and-license) 42: - [Learn more](#-learn-more) 43: ## 🚀 Quickstart 44: 1. Open the [MCP configurator](https://mcp.apify.com), pick your client, and choose the tools you want. 45: 2. Copy the generated configuration, deeplink, or command into your client. 46: 3. Sign in to Apify in the browser window that opens. If you don't have an account, you can create a free one there. 47: The hosted endpoint is `https://mcp.apify.com`. If your client can't use OAuth, send your [Apify API token](https://docs.apify.com/integrations/api#api-token) in an `Authorization: Bearer ` header instead. Treat the token like a password and keep it out of repositories. [Create a token in Apify Console](https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations) and copy it right after creating it. It is shown only once. 48: Using a coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or GitHub Copilot? An [official Apify plugin](https://docs.apify.com/agents/plugins) installs this MCP server together with [Apify agent skills](https://docs.apify.com/agents/skills) in one step. 49: ## 🤖 Set up your client 50: The [configurator](https://mcp.apify.com) generates the exact setup for each supported client, including Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude, Claude Desktop, Codex, OpenCode, Kiro, and more. The snippets below cover the most common cases. 51: ![Client setup at mcp.apify.com: tabs for Claude, Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor, ChatGPT, and more, with the Claude Code install command](docs/mcp-configurator.png) 52:
53: Claude Code 54: ```bash 55: claude mcp add apify "https://mcp.apify.com" -t http 56: ``` 57: Claude Code opens the Apify sign-in page the first time it uses the server. To install the [Apify plugin](https://docs.apify.com/agents/plugins) with Apify agent skills instead, run `/plugin marketplace add apify/apify-claude-code-plugin`, then `/plugin install apify@apify` and `/reload-plugins`. 58:
59:
60: ChatGPT 61: 1. Open [ChatGPT Plugins](https://chatgpt.com/plugins), select **Add** in the top-right corner, then **Add custom MCP server**. 62: 2. Fill in the form: 63: - **Icon**: upload the [Apify icon](https://mcp.apify.com/images/apify-icon.png). 64: - **Name**: `Apify` 65: - **Description**: `Extract data from any website with thousands of scrapers, crawlers, and automations on Apify Store` 66: - **Connection**: **Server URL**, the URL with your settings from the [configurator](https://mcp.apify.com), for example with [`?tools=`](#choose-which-tools-load). Without custom settings, use `https://mcp.apify.com`. 67: - **Authentication**: **OAuth** 68: 3. Check **I understand and want to continue**, then select **Create as a plugin**. 69: 4. Sign in with Apify, review the tools, and install the plugin. No API token is needed. 70: 5. Start a new conversation, type `@`, and select **Apify**. 71: In Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces, an admin or owner may need to create or publish the plugin. If the option is missing, ask your workspace admin. When the server's tools change, open the plugin and select **Refresh**. 72: The ChatGPT desktop app uses local MCP configuration shared with Codex instead: go to **Settings** > **MCP servers** > **Add server**, choose Streamable HTTP, and enter `https://mcp.apify.com`. See OpenAI's [custom MCP server guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12584461-connecting-custom-mcp-servers-in-chatgpt). 73:
74:
75: Cursor 76: [Add Apify to Cursor](https://cursor.com/install-mcp?name=apify&config=eyJ0eXBlIjoiaHR0cCIsInVybCI6Imh0dHBzOi8vbWNwLmFwaWZ5LmNvbS8%2FY2xpZW50PWN1cnNvciJ9), or let the [Apify CLI](https://docs.apify.com/cli) write the configuration, including your API token: 77: ```bash 78: apify mcp install cursor 79: ``` 80: The same command works for `claude-code`, `vscode`, `codex`, `kiro`, and `antigravity`. 81:

83: VS Code and GitHub Copilot 84: Use the one-click install link from the [configurator](https://mcp.apify.com), run `apify mcp install vscode`, or add `https://mcp.apify.com` as an HTTP server in your MCP configuration: 85: ```json 86: { 87: "servers": { 88: "apify": { 89: "type": "http", 90: "url": "https://mcp.apify.com" 91: } 92: } 93: } 94: ``` 95:

Use the local server when you want to run the MCP process on your own machine; Actors still run and store their results on the Apify platform in both modes. If your client supports only stdio, you can also bridge it to the hosted server with [`mcp-remote`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-remote): `npx mcp-remote https://mcp.apify.com`. 136: | | Hosted (`https://mcp.apify.com`) | Local (`npx @apify/actors-mcp-server`) | 137: | :--- | :--- | :--- | 138: | Transport | Streamable HTTP | stdio | 139: | Authentication | OAuth or Bearer token | `APIFY_TOKEN` environment variable or Apify CLI login | 140: | Output schemas inferred for Actor results | Yes | No | 141: | Tool selection | `tools` URL parameter | `--tools` flag or `TOOLS` environment variable | 142: | Updates | Always the latest server | The npm version you install | 143: ## How an agent uses Apify Actors 144: [Actors](https://docs.apify.com/actors) are serverless programs on the Apify platform. Each one does a specific job, like scraping Google Maps, crawling a website for RAG, or collecting social media posts. The MCP server turns Actors into tools an agent can find and call without you configuring each one in advance. 145: A typical task follows four steps: 146: 1. `search-actors` finds candidate Actors in Apify Store for the task. 147: 2. `fetch-actor-details` returns the Actor's input schema, README, and pricing, plus its output schema on request. 148: 3. `call-actor` starts the run and waits for it to finish, 30 seconds by default and up to 45. It returns the **run status and storage IDs**; the scraped items stay in the run's dataset. 149: 4. `get-dataset-items` reads the results from the run's dataset, with `limit` and `offset` for pagination. 150: The server adds `get-dataset-items`, `get-key-value-store-record`, `get-actor-run`, and `abort-actor-run` whenever `call-actor` or an Actor tool is loaded, so the agent can always read results and check on long runs that outlast the wait. 151: You can also expose a specific Actor as its own tool, for example `apify/instagram-scraper`. The server builds the tool's parameters from the Actor's input schema, so the agent knows exactly what to pass. A Server Actor with an API schema, such as `apify/web-fetch`, `apify/web-search`, or `apify/rag-web-browser`, gets a tool that sends one HTTP request to its API instead. 152: **Actors that run their own MCP server.** Some Actors are MCP servers themselves. `fetch-actor-mcp-tool-list` lists their tools, and `call-actor-mcp-tool` calls one. When such an Actor is loaded as a tool source and has no API schema, its tools are exposed under names in the form `username--actor-name--tool-name`; an Actor with an API schema, such as `apify/web-search`, gets its server tool instead, and `call-actor-mcp-tool` reaches its MCP tools. Apify Store also lists MCP-related Actors from independent creators; those are separate products with their own READMEs and pricing. 153: ## 🛠️ Tools, resources, and prompts 154: Any [Actor](https://apify.com/store) can be a tool, and agents discover new ones as they work. Use `call-actor-mcp-tool` with `actor`, `tool`, and `arguments`. `call-actor` still starts a run of an MCP server Actor that has an input schema; one without is refused. A selection that names `call-actor` alone needs `call-actor-mcp-tool` added. 246: - `fetch-actor-details` no longer lists an MCP server Actor's tools, and `output.mcpTools` is ignored. A selection that names `fetch-actor-details` alone needs `fetch-actor-mcp-tool-list` added. 247: - A selected Actor with an API schema (a Server Actor) gets a tool that sends one HTTP request to its API, with `method`, `path`, and `query` arguments, instead of a tool that starts a run. If the Actor is also an MCP server, the selection no longer loads its MCP tools: use `call-actor-mcp-tool`. `call-actor` still starts runs of the Actor when it has an input schema. A selected `apify/rag-web-browser` is served this way too, with `GET /search`. 248: - `apify--web-fetch` sends one HTTP request to the Web Fetch Actor's API instead of starting a run, and returns the HTTP response. Its arguments are `method`, `path`, `query` and, for `POST /`, `body`, for example `{"method": "GET", "path": "/", "query": {"url": "https://example.com", "formats": ["markdown", "links"]}}`. 249: - `apify--web-search` sends one HTTP request to the Web Search Actor's API instead of starting a run, and returns the HTTP response. Its arguments are `method`, `path`, `query` and, for `POST /`, `body`, for example `{"method": "GET", "path": "/", "query": {"query": "AI agent payment protocols", "maxResults": 5}}`. `call-actor` still starts runs of the Actor, and `call-actor-mcp-tool` calls its `search` MCP tool. 250:

With the `schedules` category loaded, "Run that Google Maps search every Monday at 9 am" creates a schedule. 283: ## 💰 Pricing and limits 284: - Connecting to the MCP server is free. Actor runs bill to your Apify account according to each Actor's pricing, which `fetch-actor-details` shows before a run. The [Apify free plan](https://apify.com/pricing) includes $5 of monthly platform usage. 285: - To cap what a run can cost, pass `maxTotalChargeUsd` (pay-per-event Actors) or `maxItems` (pay-per-result Actors) in the `callOptions` of `call-actor`. `timeout` and `memory` limit the run's duration and memory, not its price. 286: - The hosted server accepts up to 20 requests per second per account. 287: - `search-actors` returns only free and pay-per-event Actors that pass the platform's agent-safety filters, so rental and pay-per-result Actors don't appear in search. [Full-permission Actors](https://docs.apify.com/actors/running/permissions#full-permission-actors) need your one-time approval; until then, `call-actor` returns an error with an approval link. 288: - Some tools work without an Apify account: `search-actors`, `fetch-actor-details`, `search-apify-docs`, `fetch-apify-docs`, `apify-api-search`, and `apify-api-details`. Select only those, for example `https://mcp.apify.com?tools=search-actors`, and the hosted server accepts the connection without a token. 289: > 🪙 **Agentic payments (experimental).** Agents can pay for Actor runs without an Apify account. [AGI](https://agi.apify.com) sells a prepaid, spend-capped Apify API token for an x402, MPP, or Skyfire payment. The agent then uses it as a normal Bearer token against `mcp.apify.com`, with any Actor that uses limited permissions. See the [agentic payments documentation](https://docs.apify.com/agents/payments) for supported methods and limits, and [agi.apify.com/AGENTS.md](https://agi.apify.com/AGENTS.md) for protocol details. 290: ## 📡 Telemetry 291: The Apify MCP server collects telemetry about tool calls to help Apify understand usage patterns and improve the service. Telemetry is **on** by default. With telemetry on, Actor searches in Apify Store send the first 12 hex characters of the SHA-256 hash of the MCP session ID as `_traceId`, and tool-call events carry it as `trace_id`. `search-actors` also sends `_useCase`, a one-sentence reason for the search written by the model, which Apify uses to improve Store search results. The stdio transport also uses [Sentry](https://sentry.io) for error tracking, which helps the Apify team find and fix issues faster. 292: To opt out, including Sentry, set the `telemetry-enabled` URL parameter or the `--telemetry-enabled` CLI flag to `false`, or set `TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false`. CLI flags take precedence over environment variables. 293: ```text 294: https://mcp.apify.com?telemetry-enabled=false 295: ``` 296: ```bash 297: npx @apify/actors-mcp-server --telemetry-enabled=false 298: TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false npx @apify/actors-mcp-server 299: ``` 300: ## 🐛 Troubleshooting and limitations 301: - **The local server won't start.** Check your Node.js version: the package requires Node.js 22 or later. 302: - **Authentication fails.** Reconnect so the client repeats the OAuth flow, or switch to a Bearer token. For the local server, check that `APIFY_TOKEN` is set in the client's server configuration, not only in your shell. 303: - **VS Code says the OAuth app is not registered.** Run **Authentication: Remove Dynamic Authentication Providers**, select Apify, and sign in again. 304: - **Client features vary.** Any MCP client can connect, but support for dynamic tool lists, OAuth, and MCP Apps differs between clients. 305: - **Invalid Actor input.** When `call-actor` fails because of invalid input, the error includes the Actor's input schema so the agent can correct the input and retry. 306:
307: How the server adapts Actor input schemas 308: The server adapts Actor input schemas so that more clients and models can use them: 309: - Descriptions longer than 500 characters are cut at the last complete sentence and marked `[Description truncated]`. 310: - Enums are kept in full up to 2,000 combined characters. Larger enums are replaced by a short note with example values. 311: - Required fields get a `REQUIRED` prefix in their descriptions for frameworks that ignore the JSON Schema `required` list. 312: - Nested properties are built for special inputs such as proxy configuration and request lists. 313: - Missing array item types are inferred from the item type, the prefill, the default value, or the editor type, in that order. 314: - Prefill and default values are copied into descriptions as examples, for clients that ignore JSON Schema `examples`. 315:
316: For more help, see the [MCP documentation](https://docs.apify.com/mcp) or [open an issue](https://github.com/apify/apify-mcp-server/issues). 317: ## ❓ FAQ 318: **What is an MCP server?** 319: An MCP server exposes tools and data to AI agents through the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io), an open standard supported by clients such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor. The agent connects once and calls the server's tools when a task needs them. The Apify MCP server's tools are the Actors in Apify Store. 320: **What is the Apify MCP server?** 321: It's the official [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server for Apify. It lets AI agents search Apify Store, run Actors for web scraping, data extraction, and browser automation, and read the structured results. 322: **When is it a good MCP server for web scraping?** 323: When an agent needs data from many different sites. A typical case is Google Maps one day, Instagram or an online store the next. The agent picks a ready-made Actor for each site from Apify Store instead of you writing and maintaining a scraper. Each Actor works like a web scraping API for its site, and the Apify platform handles scaling, proxies, and storage of the results. 324: **How does it compare to Playwright MCP?** 325: Playwright MCP drives a browser on your machine step by step, through clicks and page snapshots. The Apify MCP server runs Actors in the Apify cloud. Each Actor handles JavaScript rendering, proxies, and blocking for its site and returns structured results, so the agent asks for the data instead of operating a browser. Many agents use both. 326: **Can ChatGPT or Claude scrape websites with it?** 327: Yes. Connect ChatGPT, Claude, or Claude Code to `https://mcp.apify.com`, then ask in plain language. The model searches for a suitable Actor, runs it, and reads the results. 328: **Is it free?** 329: Connecting is free, and some discovery tools work without an account. Actor runs bill to your Apify account at each Actor's price, and the free plan includes $5 of monthly platform usage. 330: **Do I need an API token?** 331: Not with the hosted server, because OAuth signs you in through the browser. The local server needs `APIFY_TOKEN` or an Apify CLI login. 332: **Can I limit what the agent can do or spend?** 333: Yes. Select tools with the `tools` parameter or expose a single Actor. To cap a run's cost, pass `maxTotalChargeUsd` for pay-per-event Actors or `maxItems` for pay-per-result Actors in `call-actor` options. 334: ## 🔧 Development 335: This repository contains the open-source server package published to npm as [`@apify/actors-mcp-server`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@apify/actors-mcp-server). The hosted service at mcp.apify.com runs on this core logic from a separate private repository. 336: You need Node.js 22 or later and pnpm. 337: ```bash 338: pnpm install 339: pnpm run build 340: pnpm run dev # Streamable HTTP server on http://localhost:3001, hot reload for widgets 341: pnpm run inspector:stdio # MCP Inspector against the stdio server 342: ``` 343: The development HTTP server doesn't read `APIFY_TOKEN` from the environment. Pass your token in an `Authorization: Bearer` header or a `?token=` query parameter, for example from the [MCP Inspector](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector). 344: To publish a canary build of a pull request to [pkg.pr.new](https://pkg.pr.new/), add the `beta` label to it. 345: [DEVELOPMENT.md](./DEVELOPMENT.md) covers the project structure, tool loading phases, the Node.js version policy, and testing. 346: ## 🤝 Contributing 347: Bug reports, feature requests, and documentation fixes are welcome. [Open an issue](https://github.com/apify/apify-mcp-server/issues) with steps to reproduce a bug, or describe the problem a feature would solve and who runs into it. Send typos, broken links, and wrong commands straight to a pull request. For code, work only on an issue a maintainer has invited you to pick up; unsolicited pull requests are closed. 348: Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) before you start, including the rules for [AI-assisted contributions](./CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-assisted-contributions). 349: ## 🔒 Privacy and license 350: Requests and Actor inputs go to the Apify API to run the Actors you call. Apify doesn't share them with third parties beyond what running those Actors requires. See [Apify legal documents](https://docs.apify.com/legal) for details on data collection and retention. 351: The project is licensed under the [MIT license](./LICENSE.md). 352: ## 📚 Learn more 353: - [MCP documentation](https://docs.apify.com/mcp): authentication, tool reference, and advanced configuration 354: - [Apify for AI agents](https://docs.apify.com/agents): choosing between MCP, plugins, agent skills, the CLI, and machine-readable docs 355: - [Apify agent skills](https://docs.apify.com/agents/skills): guided multi-step workflows, installed with `npx skills add apify/agent-skills` 356: - [Apify CLI](https://docs.apify.com/cli): running and building Actors from a terminal 357: - [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) 358: - [MCP for beginners](https://blog.apify.com/mcp-for-beginners/) 359: - [How to use MCP with Apify Actors](https://blog.apify.com/how-to-use-mcp/) 360: - [Webinar: Building and monetizing MCP servers on Apify](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w3AH3jIrXXo)

1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.firecrawl.dev/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # Introduction
5: > The context API for AI agents. Search the web, scrape any page, and interact with it through one API.
6: Firecrawl is the context API for AI agents. Search, scrape, and interact with the live web to get clean Markdown or structured data.
7: ## Get started
8: Connect over Streamable HTTP. The keyless server URL (Search, Scrape, and Parse; no credential required) is `https://mcp.firecrawl.dev/v2/mcp`.
9: * Codex CLI: `codex mcp add firecrawl --url https://mcp.firecrawl.dev/v2/mcp`
10: * Claude Code: `claude mcp add --transport http firecrawl https://mcp.firecrawl.dev/v2/mcp`
11: * Cursor or any JSON-config client: `{"mcpServers": {"firecrawl": {"url": "https://mcp.firecrawl.dev/v2/mcp"}}}`
12: * OpenCode (`opencode.json`): `{"mcp": {"firecrawl": {"type": "remote", "url": "https://mcp.firecrawl.dev/v2/mcp", "enabled": true}}}`
13: * ChatGPT or Claude.ai: use the native Firecrawl connector — [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/plugins?q=firecrawl) or [Claude](https://claude.ai/directory/connectors/firecrawl).
14: Both setup paths and API-key setup: [MCP Get Started](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server.md), [For Agents](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server/keyless.md), and [For Humans](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server/oauth.md).
15: ### Build directly with the API
16: Scrape your first page now. No account or API key is required for this request.
17: ```bash cURL theme={null}
18: # No API key needed to get started — add -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" for higher rate limits:
19: curl -s -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape" \
20: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
21: -d '{
22: "url": "https://firecrawl.dev",
23: "formats": ["markdown", "html"]
24: }'
25: ```
26: Add an [API key](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/api-keys) when you need higher limits. See the [Python SDK](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/sdks/python.md), [Node SDK](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/sdks/node.md), or [API reference](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/scrape.md) to build it into your application.
27: ## Other ways to get started
28: ### Install the Firecrawl CLI
29: One command installs the Firecrawl CLI, authenticates in your browser, and adds skills to every detected coding agent.
30: ```bash theme={null}
31: npx -y firecrawl-cli@latest init --all --browser
32: ```
33: > [!NOTE]
34: >
35: > Restart your coding agent after setup so it can discover the new skills. See
36: > [CLI](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/sdks/cli.md) for the full setup.
37: ### Set up with an agent
38: Provide your agent with this Firecrawl setup prompt, or see [all MCP setup options](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server.md).
39: > [!NOTE]
40: >
41: > **For AI agents:** Use [llms.txt](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/llms.txt) for an index of the documentation, or [llms-full.txt](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/llms-full.txt) for the full text.
42: ### Build and test directly
43: > [card] [Get your API key](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/api-keys)
44: >
45: > Create a free account for direct API access and higher limits
46: > [card] [Try it in the Playground](https://www.firecrawl.dev/playground)
47: >
48: > Test Firecrawl in the browser without writing code
49: ***
50: ## What can Firecrawl do?
51: > [card] [Search](#search)
52: >
53: > Search the web and get full page content from results
54: > [card] [Scrape](#scrape)
55: >
56: > Extract content from any URL as markdown, HTML, or structured JSON
57: > [card] [Interact](#interact)
58: >
59: > Continue working with any scraped page: click, fill forms, extract dynamic
60: > content
61: ### Why Firecrawl?
62: * **LLM-ready output**: Clean markdown, structured JSON, screenshots, and more.
63: * **Handles the hard stuff**: Proxies, anti-bot, JavaScript rendering, and dynamic content.
64: * **Reliable**: Built for production with high uptime and consistent results.
65: * **Fast**: Results in seconds, optimized for high throughput.
66: * **MCP Server**: Connect Firecrawl to any AI tool via the [Model Context Protocol](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server.md).
67: Bounty: 5,000 credit reward
68:  for solid feedback on Alexandria
69: To qualify, complete a high-signal interview (thoughtful, concrete use cases, etc) with our Firecrawl Feedback Assistant. Only takes a few minutes, can be stopped at any time, and is both human/agent-friendly (just paste the link into your agentic harness!). Haven't used Alexandria yet? Your take still counts.
70: [Start the interview](https://www.firecrawl.dev/survey/uilpn?src=docs-alexandria)
71: Include your email to be eligible. Interviews are reviewed for quality at the end of each week.
72: ***
73: ## Search
74: Search the web and get full page content from results in one call. See the [Search feature docs](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/search.md) for all options.
75: ```python Python theme={null}
76: from firecrawl import Firecrawl
77: firecrawl = Firecrawl(
78: # No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
79: # api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
80: )
81: results = firecrawl.search(
82: query="firecrawl",
83: limit=3,
84: )
85: print(results)
86: ```
87: ```js Node theme={null}
88: import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';
89: const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({
90: // No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
91: // apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
92: });
93: const results = await firecrawl.search('firecrawl', {
94: limit: 3,
95: scrapeOptions: { formats: ['markdown'] }
96: });
97: console.log(results);
98: ```
99: ```bash cURL theme={null}
100: # No API key needed to get started — add -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" for higher rate limits:
101: curl -s -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/search" \
102: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
103: -d '{
104: "query": "firecrawl",
105: "limit": 3
106: }'
107: ```
108: ```bash CLI theme={null}
109: # Search the web
110: firecrawl search "firecrawl web scraping" --limit 5 --pretty
111: ```

159: ## Scrape
160: Scrape any URL and get its content in markdown, HTML, or other formats. See the [Scrape feature docs](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape.md) for all options.
161: ```python Python theme={null}
162: from firecrawl import Firecrawl
163: firecrawl = Firecrawl(
164: # No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
165: # api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
166: )
167: # Scrape a website:
168: doc = firecrawl.scrape("https://firecrawl.dev", formats=["markdown", "html"])
169: print(doc)
170: ```
171: ```js Node theme={null}
172: import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';
173: const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({
174: // No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
175: // apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
176: });
177: // Scrape a website:
178: const doc = await firecrawl.scrape('https://firecrawl.dev', { formats: ['markdown', 'html'] });
179: console.log(doc);
180: ```
181: ```bash cURL theme={null}
182: # No API key needed to get started — add -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" for higher rate limits:
183: curl -s -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape" \
184: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
185: -d '{
186: "url": "https://firecrawl.dev",
187: "formats": ["markdown", "html"]
188: }'
189: ```

191: # Scrape a URL and get markdown
192: firecrawl https://firecrawl.dev

194: firecrawl https://firecrawl.dev --format markdown,html,links --pretty
195: ```

225: ## Interact
226: Scrape a page, then keep working with it: click buttons, fill forms, extract dynamic content, or navigate deeper. Describe what you want in plain English or write code for full control. See the [Interact feature docs](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/interact.md) for all options.
227: ```python Python theme={null}
228: from firecrawl import Firecrawl
229: app = Firecrawl(
230: # No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
231: # api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
232: )
233: # 1. Scrape Amazon's homepage
234: result = app.scrape("https://www.amazon.com", formats=["markdown"])
235: scrape_id = result.metadata.scrape_id
236: # 2. Interact — search for a product and get its price
237: app.interact(scrape_id, prompt="Search for iPhone 16 Pro Max")
238: response = app.interact(scrape_id, prompt="Click on the first result and tell me the price")
239: print(response.output)
240: # 3. Stop the session
241: app.stop_interaction(scrape_id)
242: ```
243: ```js Node theme={null}
244: import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';
245: const app = new Firecrawl({
246: // No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
247: // apiKey: 'fc-YOUR-API-KEY',
248: });
249: // 1. Scrape Amazon's homepage
250: const result = await app.scrape('https://www.amazon.com', { formats: ['markdown'] });
251: const scrapeId = result.metadata?.scrapeId;
252: // 2. Interact — search for a product and get its price
253: await app.interact(scrapeId, { prompt: 'Search for iPhone 16 Pro Max' });
254: const response = await app.interact(scrapeId, { prompt: 'Click on the first result and tell me the price' });
255: console.log(response.output);
256: // 3. Stop the session
257: await app.stopInteraction(scrapeId);
258: ```
259: ```bash cURL theme={null}
260: # 1. Scrape Amazon's homepage
261: # No API key needed to get started — add -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" for higher rate limits:
262: RESPONSE=$(curl -s -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape" \
263: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
264: -d '{"url": "https://www.amazon.com", "formats": ["markdown"]}')
265: SCRAPE_ID=$(echo $RESPONSE | jq -r '.data.metadata.scrapeId')
266: # 2. Interact — search for a product and get its price
267: curl -s -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape/$SCRAPE_ID/interact" \
268: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
269: -d '{"prompt": "Search for iPhone 16 Pro Max"}'
270: curl -s -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape/$SCRAPE_ID/interact" \
271: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
272: -d '{"prompt": "Click on the first result and tell me the price"}'
273: # 3. Stop the session
274: curl -s -X DELETE "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape/$SCRAPE_ID/interact"
275: ```
276: ```bash CLI theme={null}
277: # 1. Scrape Amazon's homepage (scrape ID is saved automatically)
278: firecrawl scrape https://www.amazon.com
279: # 2. Interact — search for a product and get its price
280: firecrawl interact "Search for iPhone 16 Pro Max"
281: firecrawl interact "Click on the first result and tell me the price"
282: # 3. Stop the session
283: firecrawl interact stop
284: ```

sources.numbered_text:
1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.firecrawl.dev/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # Introduction
5: > Firecrawl API Reference
6: ## Features
7: > [card] [Scrape](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/scrape.md)
8: >
9: > Extract content from any webpage in markdown or json format.
10: > [card] [Crawl](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-post.md)
11: >
12: > Crawl entire websites, extract their content and metadata.
13: > [card] [Map](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/map.md)
14: >
15: > Get a complete list of URLs from any website quickly and reliably.
16: > [card] [Search](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/search.md)
17: >
18: > Search the web and get full page content in any format.
19: ## Agentic Features
20: > [card] [Extract](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/extract.md)
21: >
22: > Extract structured data from entire webpages using natural language.
23: ## Base URL
24: All requests contain the following base URL:
25: ```bash theme={null}
26: https://api.firecrawl.dev
27: ```
28: ## Authentication
29: For authentication, include an `Authorization` header on every request except the keyless endpoints described below. The header should contain `Bearer fc-123456789`, where `fc-123456789` represents your API Key.
30: ```bash theme={null}
31: Authorization: Bearer fc-123456789
32: ```
33: `/v1/scrape` and `/v1/search` also work without a key, with limits. To call them keyless, leave the `Authorization` header out entirely, because a header with an empty token returns `401`. See [No API key (keyless)](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/authentication.md#no-api-key-keyless) for the full list.
34: To let users connect their own Firecrawl account to your app instead, use [OAuth for apps](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/oauth.md). [Authentication](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/authentication.md) compares every option.
35: ​
36: ## Response codes
37: Firecrawl employs conventional HTTP status codes to signify the outcome of your requests.
38: Typically, 2xx HTTP status codes denote success, 4xx codes represent failures related to the user, and 5xx codes signal infrastructure problems.
39: | Status | Description |
40: | - | - |
41: | 200 | Request was successful. |
42: | 400 | Verify the correctness of the parameters. |
43: | 401 | The API key was not provided. |
44: | 402 | Payment required |
45: | 404 | The requested resource could not be located. |
46: | 408 | The request timed out (e.g., page took too long to load). |
47: | 429 | The rate limit has been surpassed. |
48: | 5xx | Signifies a server error with Firecrawl. |
49: Refer to the Error Codes section for a detailed explanation of all potential API errors.
50: ### Firecrawl error codes
51: When a 408 or 5xx error occurs, Firecrawl provides more specific error codes to clarify what went wrong.​
52: | Error Code | Status | Description |
53: | - | - | - |
54: | `SCRAPE_TIMEOUT` | 408 | The page took too long to load or render. Try increasing the `timeout` parameter (up to 60000ms). |
55: | `SCRAPE_ALL_ENGINES_FAILED` | 500 | All scraping engines failed. |
56: | `SCRAPE_SSL_ERROR` | 500 | Page SSL certificate is invalid. You can use `skipTlsVerification:true` to bypass this check. |
57: | `SCRAPE_SITE_ERROR` | 500 | Unrecoverable site error. |
58: | `SCRAPE_DNS_RESOLUTION_ERROR` | 500 | DNS resolution failed. |
59: | `SCRAPE_ACTION_ERROR` | 500 | Error while performing a page action. |
60: | `SCRAPE_PDF_PREFETCH_FAILED` | 500 | Failed to prefetch PDF. |
61: | `SCRAPE_PDF_INSUFFICIENT_TIME_ERROR` | 500 | Not enough time to process PDF. |
62: | `SCRAPE_PDF_ANTIBOT_ERROR` | 500 | PDF blocked by anti-bot mechanisms. |
63: | `SCRAPE_ZDR_VIOLATION_ERROR` | 500 | Zero Data Retention conflict: occurs when `zeroDataRetention:true` but another option (e.g. `screenshot`) requires temporary storage. |
64: | `SCRAPE_UNSUPPORTED_FILE_ERROR` | 500 | Unsupported file type or file size exceeds 10MB limit. |
65: | `SCRAPE_LOCKDOWN_CACHE_MISS` | 404 | Lockdown mode is enabled but no cached data is available for the URL. Seed the cache with a non-lockdown scrape first, or disable `lockdown`. See [Lockdown Mode](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/lockdown.md). |
66: | `UNKNOWN_ERROR` | 500 | Generic or unexpected error. |
67: ## 429 responses
68: When you exceed your plan's rate or concurrency limits, the API returns a 429 response code. See [Rate Limits](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/rate-limits.md) for per-plan limits.

4: # Get Started
5: > Set up Firecrawl MCP with keyless access, account sign-in, or an API key.

13: > [card] [Use an API key](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server/keyless.md#add-an-api-key)
14: >
15: > Configure an API key in your client, no browser needed.
16: Use ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or Grok Bot? Install the native Firecrawl connector in one click:
17: > [card] [Add to ChatGPT & Codex](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugin_asdk_app_6a314a73f8ac819195b0d55e36b9c609?q=firecrawl)
18: >
19: > Install the native Firecrawl connector in ChatGPT and Codex.
20: > [card] [Add to Claude](https://claude.ai/directory/connectors/firecrawl)
21: >
22: > Install the native Firecrawl connector in Claude.
23: > [card] [Add to Grok Bot](https://x.ai/bot/plugin/789)
24: >
25: > Install the Firecrawl plugin in Grok Bot.
26: Using Claude Desktop, Cowork, or the Code tab? Follow the [Claude Desktop guide](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/quickstarts/claude-desktop.md) to connect once under the server name `firecrawl`. Setting up Grok Bot? See the [Grok Bot guide](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/quickstarts/grok-bot.md).
27: ## Sign in
28: Point your client at the OAuth server URL. Your client opens a browser window where you sign in to Firecrawl and approve a team:
29: ```json theme={null}
30: {
31: "mcpServers": {
32: "firecrawl": {
33: "type": "http",
34: "url": "https://mcp.firecrawl.dev/v2/mcp-oauth"
35: }
36: }
37: }
38: ```
39: No API key or headers are needed. Review and revoke connections from [MCP settings](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/settings?tab=mcp).
40: > [!NOTE]
41: >
42: > This is a server URL for your MCP client, not a page to open directly in a browser. API-key connections use `https://mcp.firecrawl.dev/v2/mcp` with a bearer token instead; see [Add an API key](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server/keyless.md#add-an-api-key).

47: > [card] [For Humans](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server/oauth.md)
48: >
49: > Sign in via browser.
50: Using GitHub Copilot? Follow the [Copilot CLI and VS Code guide](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/quickstarts/github-copilot.md).
51: Next: [choose a tool](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server/tools) or [run the server locally](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server/local).

107: Rate limits for different pricing plans and API requests
108: Copy pageCopy page
109: Rate limits cap how many requests your team can make per minute, while concurrency limits cap how many jobs can run in parallel. Both are set by your plan; exceeding either returns a 429 response. See Errors for the full error catalog and a retry-with-backoff snippet.
110: Concurrent Browser Limits
111: Concurrent browsers control how many pages Firecrawl can process for you in parallel. Your plan sets the ceiling; any jobs beyond it wait in a queue until a browser frees up.
112: Time spent in the queue counts against the request’s timeout parameter, so you can set a lower timeout to fail fast instead of waiting. To see current availability before sending work, call the Queue Status endpoint. Jobs that are waiting in your concurrency queue will time out after a maximum of 48 hours.
113: Current Plans
114: PlanConcurrent BrowsersMax Queued Jobs
115: Free250,000
116: Hobby550,000
117: Standard2550,000
118: Growth50100,000
119: Scale / Enterprise100+200,000+
120: Each team has a maximum number of jobs that can be waiting in the concurrency queue. If you exceed this limit, new jobs will be rejected with a 429 status code until existing jobs complete. For larger plans with custom concurrency limits, the max queued jobs is 2,000 times your concurrency limit, capped at 2,000,000.
121: If you require higher concurrency limits, contact us about enterprise plans.
122: API Rate Limits
123: Rate limits are measured in requests per minute and are primarily in place to prevent abuse. When configured correctly, your real bottleneck will be concurrent browsers. Rate limits are applied per team, so all API keys on the same team share the same rate limit counters.
124: Keyless (no API key)
125: The hosted Firecrawl MCP keyless endpoint exposes exactly Search, Scrape, and Parse without an API key. Other hosted MCP tools require an account connection or an API key.
126: For official Firecrawl clients, the CLI, SDKs, and REST API, keyless access also includes Interact. On Firecrawl Cloud, research, developer, and government search endpoints can also be used without an API key. No other endpoints (crawl, extract, map, batch scrape, etc.) are available without a key.
127: Keyless usage is free and capped per IP address per day by two limits, and exceeding either returns a 429:
128: A maximum number of requests per day.
129: A maximum number of credits per day. Operations cost different amounts of credits (for example, Interact and JSON extraction cost more than a basic scrape), so heavier usage reaches the credit cap sooner.
130: Sign up for a free API key to get 1,000 credits and higher rate limits at no cost — official clients automatically use your key once it’s configured.
131: Current Plans
132: Plan/scrape/map/crawl/search/agent/crawl/status/agent/status
133: Free10102102500500
134: Hobby100100201002050005000
135: Standard5005001005001002500025000
136: Growth50005000100050001000250000250000
137: Scale10000100002000100002000500000500000
138: These rate limits are enforced to ensure fair usage and availability of the API for all users. If you require higher limits, please contact us at help@firecrawl.com to discuss custom plans.
139: Extract Endpoints
140: The extract endpoints share limits with the corresponding /agent rate limits.
141: Batch Scrape Endpoints
142: The batch scrape endpoints share limits with the corresponding /crawl rate limits.
143: Government and Research Indexes
144: Calls to the Government Index and the Research Index are free. Each index has a per-minute limit per team that is the same on every plan:
145: IndexCalls per minute
146: Government Index300
147: Research Index100
148: Each index also has a daily call limit per team:
149: PlanCalls per index per day
150: Free / Hobby / Standard1,000
151: Growth2,000
152: Scale / EnterpriseUnlimited
153: Requests without an API key get the Free limit, counted per IP address. Counts reset at 00:00 UTC. After you upgrade, the new limit applies within about 10 minutes.
154: What counts
155: Each index has its own counts. Every call to that index counts once toward both its per-minute and its daily limit, whichever way you reach it:
156: Government Index: /search/gov, /search with the gov category, and the Government Index tool in Alexandria.
157: Research Index: every /search/research/papers endpoint (search, inspect, read and related papers), /search/research/proteins, and the Research Index tool in Alexandria.
158: A gov search on /search also counts toward your plan’s /search rate limit.
159: An Alexandria request that carries several calls to an index counts each one. If the request would go over either limit, none of its calls run. The request also counts toward the rate limit of the endpoint it is sent to.
160: A request Firecrawl rejects as invalid (400) before it reaches the index is not counted toward the daily limit, and an Alexandria request replayed with the same x-request-id is not counted toward either limit. The replay returns the saved result, except under zero data retention: no result is kept, so the replay returns 409 with code response_not_retained. A call that reaches the index counts even if the index returns an error.
161: When you reach the limit
162: Over the per-minute limit, the request returns 429 with a Retry-After header giving the seconds until the minute’s count resets. The per-minute limits are the same on every plan, so upgrading does not raise them. Over the daily limit, it returns 429 with a Retry-After header giving the seconds until 00:00 UTC. Until then, calls to that index are refused unless they fit in what is left of the daily limit or you upgrade. The daily-limit body explains the limit and how to raise it:
163: {
164: "success": false,
165: "code": "INDEX_DAILY_LIMIT",
166: "error": "Daily Research Index limit reached: your team has used 1,000 of its 1,000 calls today. The limit resets at 00:00 UTC, in 3h 12m. Upgrade to Scale or Enterprise for unlimited Research Index calls: https://firecrawl.dev/pricing",
167: "limit": 1000,
168: "used": 1000,
169: "resetsAt": "2026-10-16T00:00:00.000Z",
170: "upgradeUrl": "https://firecrawl.dev/pricing"
171: }
172: FieldMeaning
173: codeINDEX_DAILY_LIMIT from the search endpoints, index_daily_limit from Alexandria. A per-minute rate limit 429 has no code, except when an Alexandria request goes over an index’s per-minute limit, which returns index_rate_limit. Use this field to tell them apart.
174: limitYour plan’s daily limit for this index.
175: usedCalls already counted today.
176: resetsAtWhen the count resets, in UTC.
177: upgradeUrlWhere to change your plan.
178: Alexandria’s index_rate_limit and index_daily_limit responses also include retryAfterSeconds, the same value as the Retry-After header. A 429 from the rate limit of the endpoint an Alexandria request is sent to has no code; honor its Retry-After header.
179: Browser Sandbox
180: The browser sandbox endpoints have per-plan rate limits that scale with your subscription:
181: Plan/interact/interact/{id}/execute
182: Free210
183: Hobby20100
184: Standard100500
185: Growth1,0005,000
186: Scale1,5007,500
187: In addition, each team’s plan determines how many browser sessions can be active simultaneously (see Concurrent Browser Limits above). If you exceed this limit, new session requests will return a 429 status code until existing sessions are destroyed.

148: Turn any URL into clean Markdown or structured data
149: Copy pageCopy page
150: Scrape turns any URL into clean Markdown or structured data for AI agents, including JS-heavy pages and dynamic apps.
151: It manages complexities: proxies, caching, rate limits, js-blocked content
152: Handles dynamic content: dynamic websites, js-rendered sites, PDFs, images
153: Outputs clean markdown, structured data, screenshots or html.
154: For details, see the Scrape Endpoint API Reference.
155: Try it in the Playground
156: Test scraping in the interactive playground — no code required.
157: Scraping a document at a URL, or parsing one from disk? This walks through when to use Scrape and when to use Parse:
158: If a request fails, see Errors for the full catalog of error codes, causes, remedies, and retry guidance.
159: Scraping a URL with Firecrawl
160: /scrape endpoint
161: Used to scrape a URL and get its content.
162: Installation
163: Python
164: Node
165: CLI
166: # pip install firecrawl
167: from firecrawl import Firecrawl
168: firecrawl = Firecrawl(
169: # No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
170: # api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
171: )
172: // npm install firecrawl
173: import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';
174: const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({
175: // No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
176: // apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
177: });
178: # Install globally with npm
179: npm install -g firecrawl
180: # Authenticate (one-time setup)
181: firecrawl login
182: Usage
183: Python
184: Node
185: cURL
186: CLI
187: from firecrawl import Firecrawl
188: firecrawl = Firecrawl(
189: # No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
190: # api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
191: )
192: # Scrape a website:
193: doc = firecrawl.scrape("https://firecrawl.dev", formats=["markdown", "html"])
194: print(doc)
195: import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';
196: const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({
197: // No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
198: // apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
199: });
200: // Scrape a website:
201: const doc = await firecrawl.scrape('https://firecrawl.dev', { formats: ['markdown', 'html'] });
202: console.log(doc);
203: # No API key needed to get started — add -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" for higher rate limits:
204: curl -s -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape" \
205: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
206: -d '{
207: "url": "https://firecrawl.dev",
208: "formats": ["markdown", "html"]
209: }'
210: # Scrape a URL and get markdown
211: firecrawl https://firecrawl.dev
212: # With multiple formats (returns JSON)
213: firecrawl https://firecrawl.dev --format markdown,html,links --pretty
214: For more details about the parameters, refer to the API Reference.
215: PDFs and documents: /scrape auto-detects PDFs, DOCX, and other document types from URLs. Pass a PDF URL the same way you would any webpage — Firecrawl parses it and returns clean markdown. For local files that are not accessible by URL, use /parse instead.
216: Python
217: doc = firecrawl.scrape("https://example.com/report.pdf", formats=["markdown"])
218: print(doc.markdown)
219: Each scrape consumes 1 credit. Additional credits apply for certain options: JSON mode costs 4 additional credits per page, question and highlights formats cost 4 additional credits per page per format, PII redaction costs 4 additional credits per page, PDF parsing costs 1 credit per PDF page, and audio or video extraction costs 4 additional credits per page.
220: Response
221: SDKs will return the data object directly. cURL will return the payload exactly as shown below.
222: {
223: "success": true,
224: "data" : {
225: "markdown": "Launch Week I is here! [See our Day 2 Release 🚀](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/launch-week-i-day-2-doubled-rate-limits)[💥 Get 2 months free...",
226: "html": "<!DOCTYPE html><html lang=\"en\" class=\"light\" style=\"color-scheme: light;\"><body class=\"__variable_36bd41 __variable_d7dc5d font-inter ...",
227: "metadata": {
228: "title": "Home - Firecrawl",
229: "description": "Firecrawl crawls and converts any website into clean markdown.",
230: "language": "en",
231: "keywords": "Firecrawl,Markdown,Data,Mendable,Langchain",
232: "robots": "follow, index",
233: "ogTitle": "Firecrawl",
234: "ogDescription": "The API to search, scrape, and interact with the web at scale.",
235: "ogUrl": "https://www.firecrawl.dev/",
236: "ogImage": "https://www.firecrawl.dev/og.png?123",
237: "ogLocaleAlternate": [],
238: "ogSiteName": "Firecrawl",
239: "sourceURL": "https://firecrawl.dev",
240: "statusCode": 200,
241: "contentType": "text/html"
242: }
243: }
244: }
245: Response metadata and status codes
246: There are two separate status layers in a scrape response, and it helps to keep them apart:
247: API request status: the HTTP status of the Firecrawl API call itself, alongside the success boolean in the response body. An accepted and processed request returns HTTP 200 with success: true, even if the target page underneath returned a non-2xx code.
248: Page status (data.metadata.statusCode): the HTTP status the target website returned for that page (e.g. 200, 301, 404, 403, 500). This is what tells you how the page itself responded.
249: So the reliable pattern is: first confirm the request succeeded (HTTP 200 + success: true), then check data.metadata.statusCode for the actual page outcome. Firecrawl treats a statusCode of 2xx or 304 as a clean page load; anything else means the page did not load cleanly. When a page returns an error status, data.metadata.error may carry additional detail.
250: data.metadata.provider is set when a third-party data provider served the URL (see Provider-routed URLs): id is the provider that returned the data, creditsCost is what that access cost, and steps lists each provider tried, in order, with its status (matched, not_found, error) and credits.
251: Scrape Formats
252: You can now choose what formats you want your output in. You can specify multiple output formats. Supported formats are:
253: Markdown (markdown)
254: Summary (summary)
255: HTML (html) - cleaned version of the page’s HTML
256: Raw HTML (rawHtml) - unmodified HTML as received from the page
257: Raw Base64 (rawBase64) - Base64-encoded original HTTP response body; must be the only format in the request
258: Screenshot (screenshot, with options like fullPage, quality, viewport) — screenshot URLs expire after 24 hours
259: Links (links)
260: JSON (json) - structured output
261: Images (images) - extract all image URLs from the page
262: Branding (branding) - extract brand identity and design system
263: Product (product) - extract a structured product (title, price, availability, variants) from product pages
264: Audio (audio) - extract MP3 audio from supported video URLs, e.g. YouTube (returns a signed GCS URL, expires after 1 hour)
265: Video (video) - extract best-quality video from supported video URLs, e.g. YouTube (returns a signed GCS URL, expires after 1 hour)
266: Query (query, with prompt and optional mode) - ask a natural-language question about the page; the answer is returned in the answer field
267: Output keys will match the format you choose.
268: The rawBase64 format returns the original HTTP response body, encoded as Base64. The rawBase64 field holds a bare Base64 string, not a data URI. Read the MIME type from metadata.contentType. Request rawBase64 alone, because the API rejects it together with any other format. The response has no markdown, html, or rawHtml field, and it holds only the one file at that URL, not CSS, images, or other sub-resources.

683: Product object structure
684: The product object contains the following properties:
685: title: The product name
686: brand: The product brand (optional)
687: category: The product category (optional)
688: url: The canonical URL of the product
689: description: The product description (optional)
690: variants: Array of product variants. Pricing, availability, and images live on each variant — a single-SKU product still returns exactly one variant carrying these. Each variant has:
691: id, sku, title: variant identifiers and label (all optional)
692: values: a map of option name to value, e.g. { "color": "Charcoal" } (optional)
693: price: the current price object (optional):
694: amount: The numeric price value
695: currency: The currency code, reported only when the page sources it (optional)
696: formatted: The price as displayed on the page (optional)
697: sale: present only when the variant is discounted (optional). Contains:
698: originalPrice: The original (pre-discount) price, same shape as price
699: availability: availability information, always present on a variant:
700: inStock: Whether the variant is in stock
701: text: The raw availability text from the page (optional)
702: images: array of variant images, each with a url and optional alt text (optional)
703: How product extraction works
704: The product format extracts the product deterministically from on-page structured data — no LLM is involved. It merges multiple sources by priority: JSON-LD > schema.org microdata > RDFa > embedded state (__NEXT_DATA__/Nuxt/Apollo/Redux/Remix) > AliExpress runParams > GA4 dataLayer > OpenGraph/<meta>. The merge is identity-aware, so fields from different products are never combined. Currency is reported only when the page sources it.
705: Product extraction is fail-closed: ambiguous pages yield no product, and weaker sources such as OpenGraph only contribute when a price is present. On a page with no extractable product, the response omits the product object and adds a warning (e.g. “No product found…”).
706: Self-hosting: the product format is backed by a dedicated product-extraction service. On Firecrawl Cloud it works out of the box. If you self-host, set PRODUCT_EXTRACTION_SERVICE_URL to point at that service — when it is unset, requesting the product format returns a warning and no product (the same pattern the audio/video formats use for their service).

841: You can combine highlights with other formats — for example, request markdown and highlights together to get page content and source text in a single call.
842: Python
843: Node
844: cURL
845: from firecrawl import Firecrawl
846: firecrawl = Firecrawl(
847: # No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
848: # api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
849: )
850: doc = firecrawl.scrape(
851: "https://firecrawl.dev",
852: formats=[{"type": "highlights", "query": "What is Firecrawl?"}],
853: )
854: print(doc.highlights)
855: import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';
856: const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({
857: // No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
858: // apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
859: });
860: const doc = await firecrawl.scrape('https://firecrawl.dev', {
861: formats: [{ type: 'highlights', query: 'What is Firecrawl?' }],
862: });
863: console.log(doc.highlights);
864: # No API key needed to get started — add -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" for higher rate limits:
865: curl -s -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape" \
866: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
867: -d '{
868: "url": "https://firecrawl.dev",
869: "formats": [
870: { "type": "highlights", "query": "What is Firecrawl?" }
871: ]
872: }'
873: The highlights format is also available in /search via scrapeOptions, which runs the same extraction across each search result.
874: PII redaction
875: Set redactPII: true to redact personally identifiable information from returned markdown. The markdown field contains the redacted result.
876: See PII Redaction for SDK, cURL, CLI, and MCP examples.
877: Interacting with the page with Actions
878: Firecrawl allows you to perform various actions on a web page before scraping its content. This is particularly useful for interacting with dynamic content, navigating through pages, or accessing content that requires user interaction.
879: We recommend Interact over actions: our newer, more powerful way to interact with scraped pages.Interact runs as a stateful browser session that stays alive across calls, so you can drive a page turn-by-turn with either:
880: Natural language for flexible, non-deterministic flows. e.g. “search for ‘wireless headphones’, filter to 4+ stars under $200, and return the results”.
881: Playwright or agent-browser code for deterministic steps. e.g. await page.click('#export').
882: Interact also supports profiles, persistent sessions, and a live embeddable browser view (with an interactive mode where end users can drive the browser themselves).
883: Here is an example of how to use actions to navigate to google.com, search for Firecrawl, click on the first result, and take a screenshot.
884: It is important to almost always use the wait action before/after executing other actions to give enough time for the page to load.
885: Example
886: Python
887: Node
888: cURL
889: from firecrawl import Firecrawl
890: firecrawl = Firecrawl(
891: # No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
892: # api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
893: )
894: doc = firecrawl.scrape(
895: url="https://example.com/login",
896: formats=["markdown"],
897: actions=[
898: {"type": "write", "text": "john@example.com"},
899: {"type": "press", "key": "Tab"},
900: {"type": "write", "text": "secret"},
901: {"type": "click", "selector": 'button[type="submit"]'},
902: {"type": "wait", "milliseconds": 1500},
903: {"type": "screenshot", "full_page": True},
904: ],
905: )
906: print(doc.markdown, doc.screenshot)
907: import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';
908: const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({
909: // No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:
910: // apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY",
911: });
912: const doc = await firecrawl.scrape('https://example.com/login', {
913: formats: ['markdown'],
914: actions: [
915: { type: 'write', text: 'john@example.com' },
916: { type: 'press', key: 'Tab' },
917: { type: 'write', text: 'secret' },
918: { type: 'click', selector: 'button[type="submit"]' },
919: { type: 'wait', milliseconds: 1500 },
920: { type: 'screenshot', fullPage: true },
921: ],
922: });
923: console.log(doc.markdown, doc.screenshot);
924: # No API key needed to get started — add -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" for higher rate limits:
925: curl -X POST https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape \
926: -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
927: -d '{
928: "url": "https://example.com/login",
929: "formats": ["markdown"],
930: "actions": [
931: { "type": "write", "text": "john@example.com" },
932: { "type": "press", "key": "Tab" },
933: { "type": "write", "text": "secret" },
934: { "type": "click", "selector": "button[type=\"submit\"]" },
935: { "type": "wait", "milliseconds": 1500 },
936: { "type": "screenshot", "fullPage": true },
937: ],
938: }'
939: Output
940: JSON
941: {
942: "success": true,
943: "data": {
944: "markdown": "Our first Launch Week is over! [See the recap 🚀](blog/firecrawl-launch-week-1-recap)...",
945: "actions": {
946: "screenshots": [
947: "https://alttmdsdujxrfnakrkyi.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/media/screenshot-75ef2d87-31e0-4349-a478-fb432a29e241.png"
948: ],
949: "scrapes": [
950: {
951: "url": "https://www.firecrawl.dev/",
952: "html": "<html><body><h1>Firecrawl</h1></body></html>"
953: }
954: ]
955: },
956: "metadata": {
957: "title": "Home - Firecrawl",
958: "description": "Firecrawl crawls and converts any website into clean markdown.",
959: "language": "en",
960: "keywords": "Firecrawl,Markdown,Data,Mendable,Langchain",
961: "robots": "follow, index",
962: "ogTitle": "Firecrawl",
963: "ogDescription": "The API to search, scrape, and interact with the web at scale.",
964: "ogUrl": "https://www.firecrawl.dev/",
965: "ogImage": "https://www.firecrawl.dev/og.png?123",
966: "ogLocaleAlternate": [],
967: "ogSiteName": "Firecrawl",
968: "sourceURL": "http://google.com",

970: }
